If sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct reflection, then even though they hear the Tathāgata preach this Great Radiance Samādhi of Supernatural Powers, [they will not enter it].

On the contrary, they become confused and bewildered, unable to awaken and enter [the truth]. Because the Dharma is vast while their faculties are small, they cannot bear the burden upon one shoulder.
It is therefore necessary to forcibly establish steps where there are no steps, and to institute a gradual sequence within that which is without gradual stages;
only then can one attain awakening and entry.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

That you are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance, as well as the various provisional means of explanation—listen attentively now, and I shall speak for your sake. At that time, Universal...
The Bodhisattva Eye, along with the great assembly, received the instruction with joy and listened in silence.
"Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure, perfect,
and enlightened mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions."

This serves as a brief opening thread for newly initiated bodhisattvas. It employs provisional skillful means to clarify that delusion is itself awakening and that by departing from delusion, one returns to awakening.
First, it generally designates right mindfulness as the beginning of these skillful means.
"Those who seek" refers to those who give rise to a desire and seek this awakened mind. This is because both body and mind are entirely the awakened mind.

The manifestation of images—namely, that which currently possesses form and color is the body, and that which possesses discrimination is the mind—who, then, is the primordially pure awakened nature (*bodhicitta*)?
Thus, through such investigation and searching, one must desire to personally behold one's original face;
hence it is said: "one who seeks the pure, perfect circle of the awakened mind. If one wishes to investigate in this manner, one should...

One should, through right mindfulness, remain detached from all illusions. What is called "right mindfulness" means not thinking of any phenomena, but rather observing with a single mind with the intent to know that this body and mind are illusory, and further, with the intent to remain detached from all illusions.
If one knows them but does not detach, one has eyes but no feet; if one detaches but does not know them, one has feet but no eyes.
One who lacks eyes must first understand illusion and then transcend it; only when both eyes and feet are provided can one enter.
First, rely upon the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts, settle the assembly, and sit in quietude within a secluded chamber.

He constantly reflects: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements. That is to say, the hair of the head and body, the nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these colored forms return to earth.
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, foam, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the excretions of feces and urine—all these return to water.
Warmth returns to fire. Movement and transformation return to wind. Thus do the four great elements [dissolve]."

Each part being separated, one then realizes where this delusory body would be; thus one knows that this body ultimately has no substance, existing only as a phenomenon produced by combination, truly identical to an illusion or a magical transformation.
The following section correctly sets forth the skillful means. Śamatha is the training in concentration. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"If one practices śamatha, one dwells in a quiet place, sits upright in contemplation, and does not rely on the breath, nor on forms and colors, nor on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor even on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;
this is called relying on śamatha. One must maintain this firmly.
Observing the prohibitive precepts means exclusively severing external conditions and guarding the sense faculties so that they do not race outward.
Settling one’s followers means necessarily taking as companions those who share the same mind and the same practice, so that you may mutually sharpen and encourage one another.
Sitting in quietude in a still chamber means sitting in order to collect the body; for when the body abides, the mind attains peace. This must be so.
A quiet chamber is conducive because it is easy to accomplish the practice of distancing oneself from clamor.

Once the four conditions are fulfilled, one can then enter contemplation with a single mind upon a single object. First, one should observe this body with right mindfulness as a provisional combination that is without self.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "When this body is born, it is of the same category as its parents and the four great elements; at the stage of the *kalala*..."
Regarding the body: if there were only the earth element and no water element, it would be like a person grasping dry flour or ash—it could never cohere.
If there were only the water element and no earth element, it would be like oil or water—lacking solidity, it would immediately flow away and disperse.
If there were only the earth and water elements and no fire element, it would be like flesh in the shade during the summer months.
When there is no sunlight, the mass immediately flows away. If there were only the elements of earth, water, and fire without the element of wind, they would not increase.
Therefore, one great element cannot exist without the others; two great elements do not suffice, nor do three.
It is only when the four great elements are combined that they can achieve manifestation. Thus, one first observes that what is solid and obstructive is earth, and what is moist is water. Warmth...
That which heats is fire; that which moves is wind. Although this present body is seen to be a combination of the four great elements, each has its own destination.
Thus, to which great element does this deluded body ultimately belong? One thereby knows that the four great elements ultimately have no intrinsic substance;
they are merely a combination designated by the provisional name "body," and in reality are identical to illusions and transformations. To investigate in this manner is...
One knows that this body truly lacks the characteristic of a self (*ātman*). To instead identify the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as the characteristic of one's own body is an error.
Therefore, the *Aṅgirimā-bhāginī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:

"If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never, in the ultimate sense, attained a state of combination that constitutes the meaning of 'birth,' then one knows earth, water, fire, and wind."
Ultimately, not finding anything that can be separated or dispersed is the meaning of death.
The four conditions combine provisionally to give rise to the illusory existence of the six sense organs. These six organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally;
within this, illusory vital energy accumulates, appearing as if there were objective conditions, which is metaphorically named "mind. Good son, if this delusory mind...
Without the six sense objects, [the mind] cannot exist. When the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no sense objects can be found.
Within this, the conditions for the objects each return to their dissolution; ultimately, no perceiving mind can be observed.

Next, one again observes with right mindfulness that this mind is a provisional combination and lacks a self. It is precisely through the provisional combination of four conditions that the body falsely arises;
furthermore, based on this body, the six sense organs are falsely established. If one is separated from the four great elements, the six sense organs will certainly not exist;
if one is separated from the six sense organs, the four great elements will likewise not exist. Thus, there are the four great elements externally and the six sense organs internally.
Through their harmonious combination, they form a body possessed of faculties, which is termed the "root-body" (*indriya-kāya*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Due to the mutual contrast of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity is adhered to, causing vision to arise. The essence of vision reflects forms and grasps forms to form the faculty.
The fundamental source of this faculty is called the 'pure four great elements' (*mahābhūta*); for this reason, the substance of the eye is said to be like a cluster of grapes."
The pure faculties flow and rush toward the four objects, such as form and so forth; is it not the case that the body of the faculties arises from the synthesis of the internal and external?

Since the six faculties exist, they further give rise to the five consciousnesses which grasp the five objects, while the mental consciousness generally gathers the shadows of the passing-away of these five objects, accumulating them within the field of the eighth consciousness to serve as seeds; this is called *dharma*.
The mental objects (*dharmas*) serve as the objective realm for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because the mental consciousness, in perceiving these mental objects, appears to possess the characteristic of a subject that perceives, it is conventionally designated as "mind" (*citta*) by way of this false subjectivity. Below, he further traces back the perception of this mind to find it lacks intrinsic substance;
thus it is said: "This deluded mind that acts as the perceiver exists because of the six sense-objects; apart from the sense-objects, it does not exist."

It is because of objects that the mind exists. If the four great elements were decomposed until not even a single atom could be found, and within them the four elements and six sense-objects each returned to their dispersion and extinction, ultimately no perceiving mind could be seen.
Thus, there would be neither object nor mind. By investigating in this manner, one knows that this mind also has no self. And...
It was an error to previously and falsely identify the shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind.
The above concludes the explanation of the two characters "awakening to knowledge" and "illusory.
Good son, because that sentient being’s illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory...
The dust also ceases. Because the illusory dust ceases, the cessation of the illusion also ceases. Because the cessation of the illusion ceases, that which is not an illusion does not cease.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the brightness appears. Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory grime.
When the characteristics of this grime are forever extinguished, the ten directions are pure.
Below, the two characters "immediate" (jí) and "separation" (lí) are further elucidated. Here, the character "extinction" (miè) means "to distance oneself from" (yuǎnlí).
It simply refers to observing with wisdom that [phenomena] are illusory; thus, one does not falsely recognize or falsely cling to them, detaches from sensory adhesions, and inwardly subdues the mind.
To oppose manifest karma and dissolve habitual seeds is what is called "extinction"; it is not a matter of annihilating them. If it were annihilation, one would fall into [nihilism].

This is cultivated through the four formless *ākāśas*. This means that once one knows that body and mind are illusory, one should immediately distance oneself from them using the ten profound metaphors of the illusory vajra, ensuring they do not cause attachment.

One must certainly first leave behind the illusory body, next leave behind the illusory mind, and finally leave behind illusory objects. This is precisely the distancing from the extreme of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pakṣa*). Next, [one leaves behind...]
The wisdom that extinguishes illusion is precisely the distancing from the defilements of the extreme of purity.
When all illusions of defilement and purity are exhausted, yet that which is non-illusory is not extinguished—this is what is meant by "leaving illusion to attain awakening.

This is truly because sentient beings are internally driven by the mental consciousness and sustained by the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); thus, they falsely recognize each phenomenon, giving rise to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). One must necessarily eliminate [this].
When all cognitive-emotional attachments are exhausted, the luminous body of pure awakening begins to manifest. This is analogous to polishing a mirror:
only when the impurities on the mirror’s surface are completely removed does the luminosity of the mirror’s substance begin to shine forth.
Thus, we know that all sentient beings possess this luminous, pure awakening; yet it does not appear because they are like an ancient mirror that has not been polished. Yongjia said:

Hitherto, the dusty mirror has never been polished; today, it must be clearly scrutinized and analyzed. Thus, the illusory defilements of the luminous essence of awakening are fundamentally not other things;
they are simply the defilements formed by mistakenly identifying the four elements as the body and the reflected shadows of the six sense objects as the mind.
If one realizes that the four elements are fundamentally empty and that the reflected shadows are unreal, [the mind] becomes pure.
When the essence of awakening is not defiled by the view of a self-body, then the marks of impurity are extinguished and the ten directions become pure;
this is the sign that *śamatha* has been perfected.
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects the five colors, appearing differently according to the direction from which it is viewed.

Those who are ignorant see those five colors as truly existing within the maṇi. Good son, in the same way, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each type accordingly.
Those ignorant ones claim that the pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such a body and mind.
Their own characteristics are likewise thus. Because of this, they cannot distance themselves from illusion and transformation. Therefore, I say that body and mind are illusory defilements.

In contrast to those who have abandoned illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva. When defilements are exhausted and their opposites are eliminated, there is neither the defilement nor the one who speaks of it.
Good son, these Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age realize that all illusions are but the cessation of reflected images.
Therefore, at that time, one immediately attains directionless purity, which is manifested by the awakening to boundless space.
This is explained through analogy: all manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment; thus, to depart from illusion is itself awakening.
The pure maṇi jewel symbolizes the nature of pure awakening, while the five colors symbolize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Regarding the body and mind appearing differently according to each direction: it is like the five celestial kings of the directions seeing the colors of a jewel as each being different.
This is a metaphor for the five aggregates being the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

When a deluded person perceives those *maṇi* jewels as actually possessing five distinct colors, this is a metaphor for the arising of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) from the *paratantra-svabhāva*. Thus, the pure nature of *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* follows the five...

According to their respective karmic paths, they each manifest bodies and minds composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), just as a mani jewel manifests five colors according to the direction from which it is viewed.

Fools do not realize that these bodies and minds of the five aggregates are fundamentally the pure, perfect, awakened mind (*viśuddha-pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*), appearing in accordance with karma and lacking any inherent substance.
Thus, they falsely identify the nature of pure, perfect awakening as truly possessing the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) as the characteristics of their own bodies.
There are shadows conditioned by the six sense objects that constitute the manifestations of one's own mind. This is just as a fool falsely identifies a mani jewel as actually possessing five colors.
Therefore, the former masters said: "Upon the mountain peak of the five aggregates is a single expanse of emptiness; though entering and exiting through the same gate, they do not meet.
For immeasurable kalpas one has lived in a rented house, yet until the end does not recognize the master of the house. This is due to that delusion.
Failing to realize that body and mind are illusory and dependently originated, one falsely clings to them as real.
Through craving and attachment, one gives rise to love and is unable to distance oneself from these illusory manifestations and their false, cyclic flow.

Therefore, I say that both body and mind are illusory defilements manifested by the pure, perfect, awakened mind. This is because, due to the false recognition of body and mind, those who have not yet abandoned these illusory defilements remain bound.
They are called "sentient beings. Therefore, in contrast to those who have abandoned the defilement of illusion, they are called "bodhisattvas.

If the illusory defilements of sentient beings are exhausted, then even the bodhisattvas who have abandoned the defilement of illusion are eliminated. Since there are no sentient beings with illusory defilements, there are likewise no bodhisattvas who have abandoned the defilement of illusion.
Thus, one knows that both "sentient beings" and "bodhisattvas" are merely provisional designations. [This applies to] birth-and-death...
Nirvana is entirely a false designation; therefore, it is said that when all illusions are extinguished, there is no place where one attains the Way, nor is there anything attained.
Furthermore, it is said that all various illusory transformations are born from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*).

If this Bodhisattva has perfected the contemplation of illusion, then they will perceive the various illusory manifestations appearing from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment as mere shadows.
When all phenomena dependent on others are completely extinguished, one no longer falsely clings to the forms appearing in various directions as being truly existent.
At that time, one realizes the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment and immediately attains purity that is without direction.
Reaching this state, one knows that the boundless void is entirely manifested from within the heart of Great Enlightenment, just like [the waves] in the ocean.
"A single bubble—how much more so other things? This is the sign that samāpatti has been perfected.
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind manifests as pure; because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure;
because seeing is pure, the faculty of the eye is pure; because the faculty is pure, the eye-consciousness is pure; and because consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure."
Because hearing is pure, the ear-faculty is pure. Because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure. Because consciousness is pure, the perception of objects is pure.
It is thus for the nose, tongue, body, and mind as well. Good son, because the faculties are pure, the object of form is pure.
Because form is pure, the object of sound is pure; and so it is for odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

It is likewise so, son of good family. Because the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are pure, the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element (*ab-dhātu*) is pure.

It is the same for the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) and the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Son of good family, because the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are pure, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), and the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are pure.
Because those are pure, the ten powers (*daśa-bala*) and the four kinds of fearlessness (*catasraḥ vaiśāradyāni*) [are pure].

The fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are pure.
In this way, up to the eighty-four thousand doors of dhāraṇī, all are completely pure.
Good son, because the nature of all true marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure. Many...
Because the body is pure, it is thus even unto the perfect purity of the *circular enlightenment* (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) of all sentient beings in the ten directions.
Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure;
because many worlds are pure, it is thus even unto the exhaustion of empty space, wherein all things throughout the three periods of time are perfectly enveloped, equal, pure, and immovable.

Below this, the purity, immovability, and omnipresence of the enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*) are explained in detail, thereby manifesting its greatness of essence, greatness of characteristics, and greatness of function.
Since phenomena are thus liberated, the consciousnesses of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*) no longer give rise to attachment to phenomena;

they are transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which universally illumines all phenomena. As it is said: "The observation is perfectly luminous, shining throughout the great thousandfold world-system."
Therefore it is said: "Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the purity of the mind is revealed.
Only when awakening is perfectly luminous does the mind of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its discriminative functions suddenly become pure, and all things become pure.

However, because these truths cannot be manifested instantaneously, they are revealed through each successive stage of purity. Following the phrase "the mind is pure," the eighteen realms (*dhātus*) are first clarified.
"Purity. To say that the objects seen are pure means that since the mind is already pure, the forms perceived are not defiled.
That the eye-faculty is pure means that the faculty which perceives does not wander or dissipate.
That the eye-consciousness is pure means that the consciousness produced does not give rise to discrimination. This clarifies the purity of the first three realms.
"Purity. Regarding "the purity of consciousness," it means that once the first three realms have become pure, the subsequent four realms of the triple world also become pure.

Because the "perception of objects" encompasses the three realms of nose, tongue, and body, the phrase "purity of the faculties" below demonstrates that when the faculties are pure, the six objects are also pure.
The phrase "purity of the six objects" below demonstrates that when the objects are pure, the four great elements are also [pure].
It is purity. The phrase "the four great elements are pure" below reveals that while the four great elements are pure, the three realms are likewise pure.

As for what is called the "twenty-five states of existence" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*): they consist of the four continents, the four miserable destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm together with the Brahma heavens, the heaven of non-perception, and the five *anāgāmin* heavens.
The four *ārūpya-samāpattis* and the four *dhyāna*s. The above collectively clarifies the purity of worldly dharmas.
The section beginning with "That purity" further clarifies the purity of supramundane dharmas. Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*):

first is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), which means comprehensively knowing the causes, conditions, and karmic fruits of all phenomena, excluding causelessness and false causes, and knowing those who can be saved.
1. The power of knowing those who cannot be saved, and so forth. 2. The power of knowing the karmic retributions of the three periods of time;

that is, knowing the karma of the three periods as well as the three types of retribution, such as those experienced in the present life, and knowing whether those to be saved possess obstructions or lack them. 3.

The power of knowing the defilement and purity of all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, as well as knowing the various fruits obtained based upon these. 4. The power of knowing the superiority [of the five faculties], such as faith and the others.
The power of the middling and inferior [faculties]. Fifth, knowing the various inclinations and pleasures of beings, causing them to abandon the impure and increase the pure.
Sixth, knowing the various dispositions and desires regarding the One Vehicle, Three Vehicles, and Five Vehicles, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion;

knowing at once or at a later time who can be delivered and who cannot be delivered, and so forth. Seventh, knowing the destination reached by all paths. Eighth, knowing past lives. Ninth, knowing death here [and rebirth there].
Being born there is itself the wisdom of the divine eye. The tenth [power] is the knowledge that one’s own liberation is beyond doubt.

Although it is a single wisdom, it is divided into ten because it possesses ten types of functions; it is collectively termed a "power" (*bala*) because it can crush adversaries and cannot be overcome.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): the first is fearlessness in the perfect knowledge of all phenomena, which refers to the Buddha’s solemn declaration: [text continues].

1. I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge (*sarvajña*). Second, regarding the fearlessness of having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) along with their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*), I declare:

"I am free from outflows. Third, the fearlessness of declaring that there are no dharmas that obstruct the path. Fourth, the fearlessness of declaring the path that leads to the transcendence of suffering.

Regarding the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*): first, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), such as when speaking of earth, water, wind, fire, and so forth. Second...

1. Unimpededness in meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): as when explaining solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, and so forth. 2. Unimpededness in expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): this refers to employing the local dialects of those beings to explain the earth and other elements.

3. Unimpededness in eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): this is the skillful and joyful exposition based upon the three aforementioned types of knowledge. Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*):

because qualities such as the [ten] powers (*bala*) and others are partially shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), whereas these [eighteen] are not shared at all. First, the body is without... [fault].
1. No lapse in conduct; 2. no lapse in speech; 3. no lapse in thought; 4. no divergent thoughts; 5. no lack of concentration; 6. no relinquishing without full awareness;
7. no decline in aspiration; 8. no decline in vigor; 9. no decline in mindfulness; 10. no decline in wisdom; 11. no decline in liberation; 12.
no decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 13. [no decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation].
14. All bodily actions follow wisdom. 15. All verbal actions follow wisdom.
16. All mental actions follow wisdom. 17. By means of wisdom, one knows the past with unimpeded penetration. 18.
By means of wisdom, one knows the present with unimpeded penetration. 19. By means of wisdom, one knows the future.
It is unimpeded and penetrating. Regarding the "Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment" (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*): "Aid" (*pakṣa*) means assistance; they assist the Right Path.

The "Path" is precisely *śamatha* (calming) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). "Factors" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to categories, as they are of the same class as the True Cause. They are also called the "Limbs of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).

The classification is also based on their meaning. The thirty-seven [factors] refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. However, they have only ten dharmas as their substance:
namely, diligence, concentration, and wisdom each have eight; mindfulness has four; morality has three; faith has two; and pliancy, equanimity, and reflection each have one.

...Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) are: first, contemplating the body as fivefold impurity—namely, its seed, its locus, its specific characteristic, its intrinsic nature, and its ultimate state;
second, contemplating sensation as suffering; third, contemplating the mind as impermanent; and fourth, contemplating phenomena as selfless.
This serves as the antidote to the four inversions of ordinary beings. Furthermore, one contemplates the body as ultimately empty; one contemplates sensation as empty internally and externally;

one contemplates the mind as non-existent; and one contemplates phenomena as being merely names. This serves as the antidote to the four inversions of the followers of the Two Vehicles. Regarding the Four Right Efforts:
if the fire of the Four Mindfulnesses obtains the wind of diligence, there is nothing it will not consume; therefore, [the Four Right Efforts] follow next.

To analyze them: because they take diligence (*vīrya*) as their essence, they are collectively termed "diligence. Because they differ from the diligence of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they are called "right diligence" (*samyak-pradhāna*).
Although they constitute a single form of diligence, they are divided into four according to their specific functions: first, to suppress unarisen evil so that it does not arise;
second, to sever arisen evil so that it does not continue; third, to cause unarisen good to arise; and fourth, to cause arisen good to increase.

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*). "Desire" refers to aspiration; "effort" refers to uninterrupted application;

"mind" is concentration (*samādhi*), characterized by one-pointedness of object; and "investigation" is wisdom (*prajñā*), consisting of internal discernment. Through effort, one overcomes distraction.

Because the fire of wisdom is weak, one must establish fixed concentration (*samādhi*). Here, "desire" (*chanda*) refers to the sovereign power of the mind, which is itself supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). "Feet" (*pāda*) refers to concentration.

Because these four factors—desire and the others—are able to realize this [concentration] through the supreme sovereignty of supramundane dharmas, they are called the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), and are also called the bases of mastery (*ṛddhipāda*);
for desire is like the mind. The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and so forth.
Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these five faculties give rise to supramundane dharmas. The first three, when they reach this stage, are collectively termed "roots" (*indriya*).
Regarding the "five powers" (*bala*): these are simply the aforementioned five faculties in their state of growth. Because Māras, Brahmās, and others cannot subdue them, they are called "powers.
Regarding the "seven factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*): mindfulness is the factor of support; because one binds the mind through mindfulness, it causes all wholesome [states]...
All dharmas are never forgotten or lost. The discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is the factor of intrinsic nature, because it realizes specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Diligence (*vīrya*) is the factor of renunciation, because by its power one reaches the destination. Joy (*prīti*) is the factor of benefit, because through mental exultation the body becomes pliant.

Lightness, concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are all factors of non-defilement, as they are able to eliminate the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) that serve as the basis [for defilement].

Because they constitute the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), and because through equanimity of application (*upekṣā*) one eternally abandons both greed and sorrow, all seven are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Although these seven dharmas arise simultaneously in a single moment, they are each described according to their specific modes of activity (*ākāra*) and respective functions;
thus, there are seven. As for the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*): right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the factor of discernment, based upon the previously realized Truth.
Because it is the actual discernment, all [of these] are called "right. Contemplation (*vitarka*) is the branch for instructing others;
for one expresses words by establishing the names and meanings through skillful means according to what has been realized. The latter three are all branches for causing others to have faith.
Speech refers to answering questions and making definitive determinations based on what has been realized, so as to inspire confidence in others regarding the purity of one’s views.
Action refers to physical conduct—whether moving or remaining still—that is perfectly practiced, so as to inspire confidence in others regarding the purity of one’s ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Livelihood consists of seeking requisites in accordance with the Dharma and abiding by the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), being free from the five types of wrong livelihood. Diligence is that which purifies the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The limb of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the factor that purifies the hindrance of secondary afflictions, because by means of it one is forever free from all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The limb of concentration (*samādhi*) is the factor that purifies the hindrance to supreme qualities, because by means of it one brings forth immeasurable and superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). ○

Regarding the sequence of the seven aforementioned categories: having heard the Dharma, one should first recollect and uphold it; next, one should diligently practice it. Through diligence, the mind is gathered and made pliant.

Through pliancy, the faculties such as faith are established. As these faculties increase, they become powers (*bala*). The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are distinguished, and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) constitutes correct practice.
These are collectively illustrated by eight metaphors: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the earth, and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like seeds.
Right effort is the planting; the bases of psychic power are like the emerging sprouts; the five faculties are like the roots; the five powers are like the growth of the stem and leaves;
they open the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and bear the fruit of the eightfold noble path. Regarding the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs* of purity:
since there are eighty-four thousand afflictions, each one, when countered and overturned, becomes a pure dharma.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "Because one does not realize that thoughts arise and perceives various objective realms, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

This extends to encompass the meaning of all delusory defilements, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges. In contrast to this meaning, the fact that the nature of the mind is unmoving manifests the meaning of the signs of all pure merits and virtues, also numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
Question: Regarding these two characteristics of mundane and supramundane phenomena...

Question: How is it that this sutra states that all things are "pure"? Answer: If one considers them in terms of the opposition between the noble and the ordinary, there is a vast disparity in their superiority and inferiority.

However, if one contemplates them from the perspective of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), they are of one kind; they are all illusory transformations arising from conditions and lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is what is meant by "all phenomena are unattainable. That is to say, once one perceives and realizes that all worldly and transworldly [phenomena]...
All worldly dharmas are characterized by non-reality; only when one perceives the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) does one see it.

Furthermore, even the perception that there is a "true mark" to be named as such is called the purity of the true mark. One who possesses this purity of the true mark realizes the dharma of equality, which is then termed the purity of the single body.
Because of the purity of the single body, one sees that the *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment) of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions is entirely pure.
Purity. If the sentient beings of the ten directions are pure, this is called the purity of a single buddha-field.
When a single field is pure, down to every atom and every field, at all times and in all places, they are entirely equal, pure, and immovable.
This is the sign that the contemplation of *dhyāna* has been perfected.

It manifests that the ground of pure awakening is fundamentally unstained, serving as the substance for the root-bodies and the environmental world of the three periods and ten directions; thus it manifests the greatness of its essence (*tathatā*).
This is the time when one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), wherein awakening penetrates the realm of the Tathāgatas and exhausts the boundaries of Buddhahood.
Good son, just as space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.

Because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable. In this way, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors being equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.

This clarifies the realized realms from the first bhūmi up to the eighth. Having entered the first bhūmi by transforming the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) into the *suvicaya-jñāna* (wisdom of profound discernment), one subsequently enters the eighth, the Immovable Bhūmi (*acalā-bhūmi*), by transforming the seventh consciousness into the *samatā-jñāna* (wisdom of equality).
Hence it is called "equal and immovable," because all phenomena are identical to the nature of awakening. Thus...
The immovability of all phenomena is due to the immovability of the nature of awareness.

Just as space is equal and immovable, so too is the nature of awareness, for that awareness is like space. Because the four great elements are equal and immovable, the equality of the nature of awareness is likewise so.
By means of this, the Dharma abides in its own place; such is the inherent nature of a Great Man.

Because it is eternal. This reveals that the fundamental nature of pure awakening is primordially unmoving. However, one must reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and sever the innate grasping at a self associated with the seventh consciousness;
only then will the two minds of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa never arise again, and only then is it called the truly Unmoving Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Good son, because the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, pure, immovable, and perfect without limit, you should know that the six sense faculties are all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm.
Because the faculties are all-pervasive, you should know that the six sense objects are all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm.

Because the objects are all-pervasive, you should know that the four great elements are all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm. In this manner, it extends even to the gates of dhāraṇī being all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm. Good son...
Good son, because that wondrous nature of enlightenment is all-pervasive, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled.
Because the faculties and objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled, it is likewise so even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, which are neither destroyed nor intermingled.
It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room; their light pervades everywhere, being neither destroyed nor intermingled.
This clarifies the realm realized from the Ninth Ground up to Equal Enlightenment.

Since the nature of awakening is identical to all phenomena, and since this nature of awakening is pervasive and without limit, so too are the sense organs, objects, the four great elements, and even the gates of *dhāraṇī* pervasive and without limit.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Just as a single faculty of vision is pervasive..."
Pervading the dharma-realm: the ears, nose, tongue, body, and the perceptions of touch and cognition possess wondrous virtues that are brilliantly luminous and pervade the entire dharma-realm.
When stirred by the karmic consciousness of ignorance, there is discrimination; when unstirred, they are equal to and pervasive throughout the dharma-realm.

Thus, the five direct-perceiving consciousnesses and their respective faculties are each individually pervasive throughout the dharma-realm, just as when the eye perceives form, the form [is likewise pervasive].
Fundamentally, all phenomena are non-apprehendable and equal to the Dharma-realm. Thus, it is that a single mote of dust contains entire lands, and a mustard seed encompasses Mount Sumeru.

One subsumes all, and all subsume one; one enters all, and all enter one. Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, every phenomenon is unimpeded with every other, because that wondrous enlightened nature is omnipresent.
Therefore, the nature of the sense organs and the nature of the sense objects—whether large or small—are likewise so.
They do not destroy one another, nor are they intermingled. It is like a thousand lamps shining together in a single room:

the lamps differ according to their individual bowls, yet the light passes through them all; the light penetrates one another, yet each lamp remains distinct. Thus, they are eternally separate and eternally interfused. As the Sūtra says:
"To understand the infinite within the one, and to understand the one within the infinite. This is what is meant by the non-obstruction of the one and the many, which manifests pure awakening.

"Using the fundamental substance" means pervading everywhere. Herein, "pure and immovable, pervading the dharma-realm" has the same meaning as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s phrase "pure and fundamentally so, pervading the dharma-realm."
Good son, because they have accomplished awakening, you should know that Bodhisattvas are neither bound by dharmas nor do they seek liberation from dharmas;

they do not loathe birth and death, nor do they crave nirvana; they do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor do they despise those who violate them; they do not value long-standing practice, nor do they slight beginners.
Why is this? Because they are awakened to all things. It is, for example, like the light of the eye which clearly perceives objects before it; that light—
One attains the perfection of being free from hatred and attachment. Why is this? It is because the essence of light is non-dual and devoid of hatred and attachment.
This marks the transition from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) into the realm of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyaksa-bodhi*).

That is to say, by first practicing these three contemplations and realizing these three great aspects, one finally attains equal and perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena, and subsequently transforms this eighth consciousness, the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
When it becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the first five consciousnesses likewise transform into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

This is called the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) and is termed ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). Once enlightenment is ultimate, one then perceives that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are entirely equal;
therefore, one does not see any defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*) that can bind, nor does one see any pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*) that can [be attained].
Liberated, they do not perceive birth and death as something to be loathed, nor do they perceive nirvana as something to be cherished.
They do not give rise to reverence because of the observance of precepts, nor do they give rise to aversion because of the violation of prohibitions.

They do not conceive a mind of respect based on long-standing practice, nor do they conceive thoughts of contempt toward beginners. Because they have realized equality, whatever they encounter with their eyes—

All these are bodhi. Only upon reaching this point can one say that heaven and earth share the same root, that all phenomena are of one substance, that birth and death are identical to nirvana, and that ignorance is identical to buddha-nature.
Because the nature of awakening is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions, every place encountered is one's own radiance;
its essence is non-dual and gives rise to no discrimination. For example:

Just as the light of the eyes perceives objects through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*), its radiance pervades all things without attachment or aversion, because it is characterized by a single, equal nature.
This is precisely the realm of wondrous enlightenment realized by the Tathāgata.

That which is called the quiescence and equality of body and mind, the fundamental limit (*koṭi*) that is perfectly fulfilled throughout the ten directions, non-dual and compliant—its essence is just like this.
"Good son, for this Bodhisattva and those sentient beings of the final age who cultivate this mind and achieve its perfection, there is neither cultivation nor achievement.
Perfect Enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent extinction, non-dual.
Within it, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* unspeakable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise like scattered flowers in the sky."
Chaos is extinguished; it is neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor liberated.
Only then does one know that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, and that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.

Good son, because they are like a dream from yesterday, you should know that birth-and-death and nirvana are without arising or ceasing, without coming or going. That which is realized is without gain or loss, without grasping or rejecting.
It is relinquishment. That which can realize it is without activity, without cessation, without effort, and without extinction. Within this realization, there is neither subject nor object;
ultimately, there is neither realization nor one who realizes. The nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible. Good son!
Those bodhisattvas, practicing in this way, progressing through these stages, contemplating in this manner,
maintaining themselves in this way, employing such skillful means, and attaining awakening in this fashion, seek such dharmas without becoming confused or distressed.

When a Bodhisattva has cultivated this mind to the point of ultimate perfection, pervading the worlds of the ten directions, then body and mind are stilled, and self and other are mutually integrated, attaining true abiding and sustenance.

Only then can it be said that one does not perceive a "self" as the person who achieves, nor an "enlightenment" (bodhi) as the dharma to be achieved. Through this, that karmic consciousness is transformed into Great [Enlightened Wisdom].
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). By means of this mirror wisdom, one perceives that all root-bodies, faculties, and the vessel-worlds are entirely quiescent, equal, and non-dual.

That is to say, within the great, perfectly round, and stainless [wisdom] that simultaneously radiates light universally illuminating the lands and atoms of the ten directions, one sees the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arising and ceasing in disorder within the mind of wondrous enlightenment, just like a madman.

Just as flowers in the sky arise and perish in confusion, one is further able to perceive that all sentient beings are neither identical to Perfect Enlightenment nor separate from Perfect Enlightenment.
There is no dharma of birth and death by which they can be bound, nor is there any dharma of nirvana by which they can be liberated.
Upon reaching this point, one finally knows that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, not requiring cultivation or realization. Thus, at the beginning, the World-Honored One...
Upon attaining perfect enlightenment, he marveled, saying: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they fail to realize it.
Looking back, all the various arduous efforts I previously made—desiring to sever birth and death and to realize nirvana—were merely realms manifested within a dream."
Once awakened, one realizes that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally unobtainable.
Knowing this to be a dream, one understands that nirvāṇa has never arisen, birth-and-death has never ceased, nirvāṇa originally has no coming, and birth-and-death originally has no going.
As for the Dharma realized therein, it was never gained at the time of awakening, nor was it ever lost during delusion. At the time of awakening...
It was never grasped; when deluded, it was never abandoned. The person who can realize this is likewise far removed from the four maladies:
they do not take the performance of various illusory practices as realization and cling to them as such; they do not take the pursuit of stillness as practice and cling to it as realization;
they do not take all things occurring spontaneously as realization and cling to them as such; nor do they take all things in their state of quiescence [as realization].
Yet one clings to this as that which can realize [enlightenment]. Within the essence of Perfect Enlightenment (Pūrṇabodhi) thus realized, not even a hair’s breadth is established.
To direct the mind toward it is immediately to err; to stir a thought is immediately to create a separation. Therefore, there is no dharma to be realized, nor is there a Buddha who realizes.
Thus, a verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "In all things there is no nirvāṇa; there is no Buddha of nirvāṇa, nor is there a nirvāṇa of a Buddha."
It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened. Furthermore, the preceding text states: "When all illusions have ceased, there is no place;
even the attainment of the Way is non-attainment. This is because the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally equal and indestructible.

Therefore it is said: "True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and sentient beings are merely designations. Thus, he concludes and demonstrates: "If this is so..."

The Bodhisattva takes this pure awakened mind as the foundation for practice. With single-minded observation, they regard the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world as being like illusions, serving as the implements for cultivation.
Finally, by departing from all illusions, they enter the pure awakened mind as the state of abiding and sustenance.
This is the establishment of a provisional sequence within that which is without sequence, and the establishment of provisional means within that which is without means.

This establishes the skillful means (*upāya*). If one can thus gradually reveal, gradually practice, and gradually realize [the truth], one will certainly not become confused or bewildered and fail to enter [the path].

Upon reaching this point, it becomes clearly understood that the first chapter [of the *Awakening of Faith*] relies entirely upon the pure aspect of *bodhi* (enlightenment) within *pariniṣpanna-jñāna* (perfected wisdom);
only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way. As for the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*...

That is to say, because there is fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), there is non-enlightenment; and because there is non-enlightenment, there is initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). It is thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "O Universal Eye, you should know: all..."
The bodies and minds of all sentient beings are entirely like illusions. The physical form belongs to the four great elements; the nature of the mind returns to the six sense objects.

Since the substances of the four great elements are each separate, who is it that brings them together? By practicing in this way gradually, everything becomes completely pure. It is unmoving and pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
there is no acting, stopping, relying, or ceasing, nor is there anyone who can realize it. All Buddha-worlds are just like...
Like flowers in the sky, the three periods of time are entirely equal, ultimately without coming or going.
Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment, as well as sentient beings of the final age who wish to enter the Buddha-way, should practice cultivation in this manner.
All sentient beings falsely identify the four great elements and the shadow-like reflections of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of body and mind.

They do not know that both body and mind arise from the delusion of the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñāna*), which produces the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). This illusorily brings forth the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the body-mind complex, which fundamentally lack any substantial reality.
If one observes each of these individually, one will realize that the characteristics of the body belong to the four great elements, and the body itself...
There is no body. The characteristics of the mind return to the six sense objects, yet the mind is fundamentally without mind.

Since the four great elements are each separate, who is there to bring them together to constitute a "self"? Thus, when this grasping at a self is empty, the conceptual grasping at phenomena is also exhausted.
When conceptual grasping at phenomena is exhausted, the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world are all entirely pure, and one attains entry into the first [stage].
From the first bhūmi, one gradually severs the innate clinging to dharmas (*sahaja-dharmagrāha*) and enters the Immovable Bhūmi (*acalā-bhūmi*).
From the Immovable Bhūmi, one gradually enters the Equal and Wondrous [Bhūmis]. Thus, the nature of awakening becomes perfect and all-pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*.

Upon reaching this state, the four maladies regarding the dharma realized are simultaneously abandoned. Since one no longer perceives any dharma that is realized, nor does one perceive any agent who realizes it.
When realized by a person, one reflects that all Buddha-lands are like flowers in the sky, and that all three periods of time—past, future, and present—are devoid of coming or going.
This is precisely what a Bodhisattva realizes through gradual stages until reaching the ultimate fruit.
Those who have first resolved their minds to seek entry into the Buddha-way should practice in this manner; thus they will forever sever ignorance and attain entry.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have skillfully proclaimed for the sake of all the bodhisattvas the gradual practice of the causal ground according to the pure Great Dharani of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment."

Next, as for the skillful means: [the Buddha] opened up the ignorance and delusion of all sentient beings. The assembly of Dharma followers, receiving the World-Honored One’s compassionate instruction, found their illusory cataracts cleared away and their eyes of wisdom purified.
"World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, why is there still the existence of all-encompassing ignorance?
If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further..."

It is taught that they have been enlightened from the very beginning. While ordinary beings of the ten directions originally attained the Way of Buddhahood and subsequently gave rise to ignorance, when could all Tathāgatas ever again give birth to any afflictions?

I only pray that you will not abandon your unimpeded great compassion, but reveal the secret treasury for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and so that all sentient beings of the final age may hear such a sūtra as this.
Having spoken these words to forever sever doubt and regret regarding the definitive teachings of the Dharma, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
He made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
Because all sentient beings have been Buddha from the very beginning, he feared that people might harbor doubts; thus, this Bodhisattva was able to...
Vajrabodhi severed people’s doubts; therefore, seizing the opportunity, he posed questions. This is what is meant by saying that a sword, due to its imbalance, leaves its precious scabbard.

In the passage beginning with "The skillful," he praises the Tathāgata for his excellent exposition of expedient means. In the section beginning with "World-Honored One," he formally presents three doubts.
The first doubt is: if sentient beings have been Buddha from the very beginning, then ignorance should not exist. This...
To know that [the nature] is unchanging while not knowing that it accords with conditions is a form of attachment. Second, the doubt:
"If ignorance were originally present, then one should not say that one is originally enlightened. Why, then, do you further say that sentient beings are originally enlightened?

This is the attachment of knowing that [the nature] accords with conditions while not knowing that it is unchanging. Third, the doubt: "If it is said that ordinary beings throughout the ten directions are originally..."
If one were to give rise to ignorance after having already attained Buddhahood, then once all Tathāgatas have become Buddhas, at what time would they ever again give rise to all afflictions?
This would mean that birth could become Buddhahood, and Buddhahood could likewise become birth;
this is the deluded attachment of confusing the ordinary with the sage. This very knot of doubt is truly a vajra-ring and a thorny *liji* fruit—how can it be swallowed?
Neither entering nor exiting, neither vomiting nor exhaling—this is the manner in which sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age give rise to the state of doubt while practicing Chan meditation.
It is no different from Huanglong’s Three Barriers (Sanguan). Alas, it is regrettable that the World-Honored One has, without cause, broken the seal by providing commentary.

As for the "Secret Treasury" (Bimi zang), it means that this Dharma-gate is realized by all sentient beings together, yet sentient beings do not know it; therefore, it is said: "It is fully possessed within the dharma of ordinary people."
Ordinary beings do not know it; though they possess the qualities of the noble ones, the noble ones do not encounter it.

When this treasury has not yet been opened, there are thousands of hardships and ten thousand difficulties. Yet once it is opened, it does not take more than the snap of a finger. One must have the key in one's own hand before it can be attained.
As for what is called the "Dharma-gate of the Definitive Meaning," it means that if one opens the door to this treasury, [the truth] is exhausted all at once.
When one sees the fundamental substratum and there is nothing further to conceal, then one’s doubts are severed and one’s regrets are exhausted.
For doubt (vicikitsā) has the nature of hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths, and its function is to obstruct faith.
Regret (kaukṛtya), on the other hand, consists of remorse for both good and evil deeds, whereby the mind becomes unsettled.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound, secret, and ultimate skillful means.
This is the supreme instruction for bodhisattvas, the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna, which enables those who practice in the ten directions..."
“May the Bodhisattvas in training and all sentient beings of the final age attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake. At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having received these instructions, rejoiced, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.
"Decisive faith" means having the firm conviction that one has been a Buddha from the very beginning and need not seek it elsewhere.
This is like what Damei said: "Let you be 'neither mind nor Buddha'; I am simply 'this very mind is Buddha,'" and so forth.

"Good son, all worlds—beginning and end, birth and death, before and after, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, arising and ceasing—succeed one another in every thought-moment, revolving and returning in cycles.

All such various acts of grasping and rejecting are saṃsāra. To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) while not yet having emerged from saṃsāra is for that nature of Perfect Enlightenment to likewise participate in the flow [of transmigration]. There is no possibility of escaping saṃsāra in such a state. It is, for example,"
It is like moving one’s eyes, which causes the clear water to appear to sway; or like fixing one’s gaze while spinning a firebrand, which creates the illusion of a wheel of fire.
It is just the same when clouds move and the moon appears to travel, or when a boat moves and the shore seems to shift.

Good son, if those objects cannot even be found to abide first while the spinning has not yet ceased, how much less so can one contemplate the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment with a mind revolving in the defilements of birth and death that has never been purified?
[The Buddha] turned back [the discourse]. Therefore, you have given rise to three delusions.

First, I shall answer your primary doubt: You say that while the nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence is fundamentally without beginning or end, nor any matter of birth, death, or saṃsāra, there nevertheless exist such things as beginning, end, birth, death, and so forth.
All of these are simply the karmic consciousness following six kinds of causes and conditions.
The continuity forms the mind of saṃsāra; thus, there is indeed revolving. "World" refers to temporal flux, and "realm" refers to spatial orientation;
that is to say, at all times and in all places, everything flows and revolves by means of these six causes. Regarding "beginning and end":
this refers to seeds giving rise to manifest activity, taking the seed as the beginning and manifest activity as the end. This corresponds to the cause of existence (*bhava-hetu*).
Furthermore, "arising and ceasing" refers to the arising of seeds from present activity and the ceasing of present activity as it flows into the future to function as seeds.
This is the cause of continuity. These two types [of causes] constitute the direct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Preceding and succeeding" refers to a preceding moment of consciousness inducing a succeeding moment; this is the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Because it exists between cause and effect, acting as an uninterrupted continuity that opens the way for the subsequent state, it is a "conditioned by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*). "Existence and non-existence" refers to the mutual arising of mind and mental objects (*ālambana*);
when one exists, both exist, and when one is absent, both are absent. This is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This is what is being demonstrated.

This refers to the cause. As for "gathering and dispersing," it means that when conditions assemble, there is gathering; when conditions separate, there is dispersal. This refers to the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of various types of karma.
It is like a wheel-turning monarch who, through his superior power, performs acts of predominance; this is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

As for "ceasing and arising," it means that only after the aforementioned various conditions have ceased can [the result] arise; this is the dependent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*). This includes the preceding...
The four conditions bring about contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Possessing the final one of these conditions brings about uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Now it is said that the Tathāgata’s nature of quiescent extinction is fundamentally free from defilement; yet, by following defiled conditions, it becomes defiled.

It is fundamentally free from purity; yet, by following pure conditions, it becomes pure. In this way, defilement and purity continue in succession from moment to moment, revolving and returning in a cycle.
Some grasp at the defiled while abandoning the pure; others abandon the defiled while grasping at the pure.
Thus, whether the mind is stirred or stilled, it revolves within the cycle of beginning and end, arising and ceasing.

If one were to abandon the six causes, transform the eight consciousnesses, exhaust the two obstacles, and transcend the two deaths such that the nature of saṃsāra no longer exists, then one would know that the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally unmoving.

If the six causes have not been exhausted, the eight consciousnesses have not been transformed, the two obstacles have not been eliminated, and one has not emerged from the two modes of death, then while within saṃsāra, one attempts to discern the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Although that nature of perfect enlightenment is quiescent and immovable, it nevertheless flows and turns according to the two conditions of defilement and purity. Being within saṃsāra, one becomes stuck and attached at every point; thus it is said:
It is impossible for one to escape saṃsāra [if one does not realize this]. Below, four metaphors are used to clarify that the pure, perfect *bodhicitta* is fundamentally without transmigration;
it is only through the eight consciousnesses that transmigration occurs.

"The still water can be shaken by the movement of the eyes" means that while the still water is unmoving, one perceives the still water as moving because of the movement of the eyes. This metaphor illustrates that the wondrously profound nature of awakening is fundamentally...

Movement. Because of ignorance, this single movement transforms into the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), and thus the wondrously profound enlightened nature also moves along with that karma-consciousness.
Regarding "the fixed eye revolving due to fire": "due to" refers to the cause. Fire itself has never undergone revolution.
Because of the fixed eye, one sees a fire-wheel revolving; this is a metaphor for how the nature of awakening is fundamentally without transmigration.
Due to the fixed grasping of the seven consciousnesses as a self, one perceives transmigration according to what arises and to what one is bound. Thus, Tanzi said:
When looking at a swirling current, one’s own head seems to spin; when performing a circular dance, the palace buildings all seem to rotate.
As for the phrase "the clouds move and the moon travels," it means that the moon itself does not actually race along, but because the clouds move, the moon appears to race.

This serves as a metaphor for the nature of awareness (*jñāna-svabhāva*), which turns spontaneously and has never actually flowed away; yet because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) races and rushes toward various objects, one perceives the nature of awareness as doing so.

This too is merely a drifting current. As for the saying that "the bank moves as the boat travels," it means that the bank does not actually move; rather, because the boat is moving, one perceives the bank as moving.

This is a metaphor for the fact that the nature of awareness (*buddhi*) is fundamentally non-transient, yet because the first five consciousnesses shift according to their objects, one perceives the nature of awareness as shifting as well.
From this, one should know that when the eyes move, the still water will necessarily appear to ripple.
If one seeks that which does not waver, it cannot be found. One whose eyes are fixed sees a whirling fire-brand;

if one seeks that which does not turn, it cannot be found. When clouds race across, the moon appears to move; if one seeks that which does not move, it cannot be found. When a boat travels, the shore appears to shift;
if one seeks that which does not shift, it cannot be found. If even material objects are thus, how much more so is the case with birth?
Within the eight kinds of defiled consciousness that revolve in the cycle of death, there has never been a single moment of purity.
Yet, by observing with this impure mind, can one find a pure awakening that does not follow the flow of transmigration?

Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas; because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, there exists all-encompassing ignorance.
It arises. You do not understand this meaning; you falsely perceive cyclic existence where there is no cyclic existence, and you falsely give rise to the three delusions where there is no delusion.
The three delusions refer to the delusions of views, thought, and dust-sand, as well as fundamental ignorance.
It is not necessarily the case that the "three delusions" refers specifically to the three doubts.
Good son, it is like an illusory cataract causing one to falsely perceive flowers in the sky.

If the illusory cataract is removed, one cannot say that this cataract has been extinguished and will arise again at some future time. Why is this? Because the two dharmas—the cataract and the flowers—are not [substantially] distinct phenomena.
Because it is dependent [upon conditions]. It is also like the extinction of flowers in the sky: one cannot say that empty space will ever again give rise to flowers.
Why? Because space originally has no flowers; they neither arise nor perish.

Birth-and-death and nirvana are alike in arising and perishing, whereas wondrous enlightenment’s perfect illumination is free from the cataracts of such flowers. Good son, you should know that empty space is not something that exists only temporarily.
Nor is it merely temporarily non-existent; how much less so for the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, which accords with reality as the equal nature of empty space?

This is the answer by analogy to the third doubt. The cataract is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*); the flowers are a metaphor for the body and mind. When the cataract arises, the flowers arise; when the cataract ceases, the flowers cease.
If the cataract had ceased, one would have to wait for a cataract to arise again; if the flowers had ceased, one would have to wait for the flowers to arise again.
To say they arise is truly the mark of madness and delusion.
Since the two phenomena of the cataract and the flower originally have no seeds, once the cataract has ceased in the eye, one cannot further wait for when it might arise again within the eye.

It is just as when flowers in the sky have already vanished from the void; one should not further wait for when those delusional flowers might arise again within the void. Why is this? Because the void...

Fundamentally there are no flowers; since even their arising does not exist, how could their cessation be possible? Thus we know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are identical to the arising and cessation of cataract-induced flowers.
If one considers the mark of the perfect illumination and pure awakening of sentient beings, even the two marks of ignorance and the cataract-induced flowers of body and mind cannot be found;
how much less so once one has already attained Buddhahood and realized this purity?

Can one who has awakened to the ground of enlightenment give rise to afflictions again? You should know that the flowers seen by those with cataracts may be said to exist momentarily and then cease to exist momentarily within empty space.
However, if empty space is eternal and unchanging, how could it be said to exist momentarily and then cease to exist momentarily?
If even empty space cannot be said to exist momentarily and then cease to exist momentarily, how much less so can the Tathāgata, who accords with perfect reality?
When awakened, it is the equal nature of empty space; thus, one may speak of it as being momentarily present and momentarily absent, yet one asks:
"When could ignorance and afflictions ever arise again? By means of this single analogy, it is revealed that the nature of awakening is fundamentally without cultivation or realization.
Good son, it is like refining gold ore: the gold does not exist because of the refining; once it has become gold, it cannot be turned back into ore.
Even after an infinite period of time, the nature of the gold is not destroyed. One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is also like this.

This is answered by means of a metaphor regarding the second doubt. If it is argued that since ignorance (*avidyā*) exists fundamentally, one should not further say that one has been a Buddha from the beginning, the metaphor is as follows:
suppose there is a person who opens a large furnace and smelts ore to produce gold.
However, the gold within the ore already existed inherently within the ore; it does not come into being merely because of the smelting. It causes the ore to be completely transformed [into gold].
Gold, once it has become gold, will certainly never again become ore; even after an infinite period of time, the nature of gold will certainly not change or perish.
Although this gold emerges from smelting, one should not say that this gold did not originally exist within the ore.
The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is like pure gold within the ore of ignorance; it must be purified through the complete exhaustion [of the defilements].

It is through ignorance that the nature of awakening first manifests; yet this nature of awakening is inherently present within the ore of ignorance from the very beginning, not something that comes into being solely as a result of eliminating ignorance.
Once the ore of ignorance is exhausted and the pure nature of awakening is realized, that pure nature of awakening will certainly never again give rise to ignorance.
Thus, even throughout immeasurable kalpas, the nature of awakening remains indestructible. Although...
The awakened nature emerges from the dissolution [of ignorance]. One must never say that this awakened nature does not inherently exist within the ore of ignorance;
otherwise, how could one say that it is "originally the Buddha"? Therefore, it is said: "The sage is originally made from an ordinary person.
If an ordinary person did not possess the nature of a sage, there would never be an opportunity for them to attain Buddhahood. From this...
This analogy illustrates that the nature of awakening involves both cultivation and realization.
Good son, within the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa;
nor is there the attainment of Buddhahood or the failure to attain it; nor is there deluded saṃsāra or the absence of saṃsāra. Good son, it is merely that all...
The realm perfected by the śrāvakas is one in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished;

yet they can never reach the nirvāṇa manifested through the direct realization of that [Tathāgata]. How much less could they fathom the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment with a mind of discursive thought?
It would be like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s light—it could never ignite it. With a mind of saṃsāra, one gives rise to saṃsāra...
Turning back, one sees that it is impossible to reach the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa.

For this reason, I say that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra. Good son, any conceptualization involving volitional effort arises from the mind;
these are all the illusory vapors of the six sense-objects and are not the true essence of the mind, as has already been explained.
"Flowers in the sky. To employ such contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha is like attempting to produce empty fruit from flowers in the sky;

it is a case of successive delusions, and such a thing is impossible. Good son, this vain and floating mind, with its many clever views, cannot accomplish the expedient means of Perfect Enlightenment.
Such discrimination does not constitute a correct inquiry.
From here below, the pure nature of awakening (*bodhi-citta*) is directly revealed as cutting off both extremes, not established even by a hair’s breadth.
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is transformed, it is designated as "awakening" (*bodhi*); because birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is transformed, it is termed "nirvāṇa.
Since these are relative phenomena, if one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally empty and birth-and-death is fundamentally quiescent, there is nothing to be realized.
There are no marks (*lakṣaṇa*), nor even the name of "realization. Therefore, there is neither the matter of attaining Buddhahood nor failing to attain it;
nor is there any discourse on saṃsāra or non-saṃsāra. This is because this pure awakened mind is free from all names and marks. Thus, the *Zongjing* asks:
"If one directly realizes that this mind is Buddha, must one further undergo the eight phases of attaining the Way? The answer is:
