If one realizes that this mind is itself the True Heaven-Born Buddha, there is no talk of attainment or non-attainment.
To speak of "becoming a Buddha" is merely a figurative expression, a supplementary designation. Thus it is said: "The Dharma-body is awakened and realized; there is not a single thing.

The fundamental source, the original nature, is the True Heaven-Born Buddha. Having thus directly pointed it out, he further rebukes them, saying: "Moreover, even the śrāvakas possess this self-nature."

One may perfect and purify the realm of meditative states; yet, by dismembering the physical body, discarding intellectual acuity, severing speech, and stilling thought, such cultivation leads only to a liberation of ash-like extinction and quiescence.
Ultimately, one cannot reach that primordial state of personally realizing the self-nature—the pure, empty, and tranquil realm of nirvana. How much less so, if one relies on [the existence of]...
To attempt to fathom the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment through the deliberations of the conceptual mind is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow;
it can never set it ablaze. If it were a true fire, a single spark could consume the entire earth, let alone Mount Sumeru.
Now, if one gives rise to the mind of saṃsāra and harbors the views of saṃsāra while desiring to enter the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, one will ultimately be unable to reach it.
However, if for a single thought-moment one realizes that dependent origination is non-arising and ignorance is suddenly severed, then in the mere twinkling of an eye one attains awakening and entry.
How could this wait for long? Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to achieve the Buddha-way must first sever [ignorance] from the beginningless past.
The root of saṃsāra. Furthermore, he rebuked him, saying: "Deliberate thoughts arise from the existence of a mind;
they are all false imaginings and dependent shadows produced by the six sense-objects, not the true essence of the mind. They are entirely like flowers in the sky."
Therefore, to seek to discern the realm of non-arising and non-ceasing through the contemplation of arising and ceasing is like inviting a flower in the sky to produce fruit from the sky;
it is merely a process of successively increasing delusive thoughts—how could such a thing ever be achieved?
Furthermore, this conditioned contemplation is empty and not substantial, false and not true, superficial and not profound; thus, it abounds in clever contrivances.

They engage in forced interpretation and conceptual measurement; they do not know that those who cultivate Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti’s *Awakening of Mahāyāna*) strictly avoid such antiquated trappings.
Only those who are utterly simple, innocent, unassuming, and obscure—having nothing at all to grasp and being incapable of anything—are able to enter.
Therefore, it is further rebuked, saying: "These three kinds of discrimination and conceptualization are all [the workings of] the multitude..."
To give rise to a distorted view is not a correct question. The question asks: "The Tathāgata initially praised that which was asked as being a profound and secret skillful means;
why then does he now reprove him for having many clever views and call it an incorrect question?"
Answer: To praise is to extol its initiation; to censure is to dissolve its cognitive views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "O Vajragarbha, you should know:
the Tathāgata’s nature of quiescence has never had beginning or end. If one contemplates it with a mind of saṃsāra, it immediately revolves back. But upon reaching..."
One cannot enter the ocean of the Buddhas from within the bounds of saṃsāra. It is like gold ore that has been smelted;

although the gold was not nonexistent because of the smelting, it is nonetheless fundamentally gold that is finally perfected through the process of smelting. Once it has become the substance of pure gold, it will never again become ore.

Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are equally like the appearance of flowers in the sky. Even contemplation is like an illusion or a transformation; how much more so [the rest]?
This refutes falsehood. If one can thoroughly understand this mind, only then should one seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

The Tathāgata’s nature of quiescent extinction is fundamentally without beginning or end, nor does it possess birth or cessation. It is only because sentient beings have not yet escaped saṃsāra that they use the conceptualizing mind to discern the realm of the Buddha;
thus, they follow that conceptualization and likewise undergo cyclic revolution. This is simply a matter of...
If one enters the cycle of saṃsāra, one cannot enter the ocean of the Buddhas.
Therefore, although sentient beings are by nature originally enlightened, because they have entered the ocean of ignorance, they wander and flow along with its waves.

If one can forever sever ignorance, the awakened nature will manifest of itself. Nevertheless, it cannot be said that the pure awakened nature does not exist within the ocean of ignorance from the very beginning.
It is just as when ore is smelted to produce gold. This gold was originally inherent within the ore; it does not come into existence because of the smelting.
Nevertheless, although it is inherently present, it must depend upon the removal of the ore to become gold. Once the essence of the gold is fully realized, it can never again become ore.
Therefore, it is said that while Buddhahood is fundamentally present, one must diligently cultivate it; while delusions are originally non-existent, they must be severed. Although...
Nevertheless, this is also a teaching given through the skillful means of the second gateway.

If one refers to the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind—the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—wherein from the beginning there was never such a thing, then both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally illusory cataracts;
sentient beings and Buddhas are all but empty flowers. It is because of your initial stirring of thought and reflection that these are but illusions and transformations.
This is the very root of saṃsāra. Why abandon this and instead interrogate its illusory manifestations? Is that not an error?
If one can understand that such conceptualization is itself an illusion and the root of saṃsāra, only then may one seek Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi).

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Miquin rose from his seat amidst the great assembly. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have extensively opened the secret treasury for the sake of the bodhisattvas, enabling this great assembly to deeply awaken to saṃsāra and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, so as to be able to bestow [benefit] upon all in the final age."
Sentient beings possess the fearless eye of the Way and give rise to decisive faith in Great Nirvana;

they no longer follow the realms of saṃsāra nor give rise to views of cyclic existence. World-Honored One, if Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s quiescent extinction, how should they sever the root of saṃsāra? Within all forms of saṃsāra, how many kinds are there?

Regarding the nature [of reality], how many distinctions are there in the cultivation of the Buddha’s Bodhi? When returning to enter the realm of worldly toil, how many kinds of skillful means of instruction should be established to deliver all sentient beings?

We pray that you will not abandon your great compassion for the world, so as to cause the eyes of wisdom of all practicing Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age to be cleared and purified, illuminating the mirror of the mind and enabling them to perfectly realize the unsurpassed [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
"Knowing and seeing. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. He made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
The preceding four chapters have already extensively distinguished "mind-only" for the sake of Bodhisattvas of the Sudden Teaching, concluding the revelation of the awakened mind in the causal stage.
Hereafter, for the sake of Bodhisattvas of the Gradual Teaching, [the text] further investigates the root of saṃsāra in depth, extensively discussing "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) to...

This reveals the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). If one knows that all is mind-only (*cittamātra*) but fails to penetrate consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one will have a superficial and vague understanding of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Therefore, Maitreya, seizing the opportunity, poses a question to investigate and exhaustively analyze the distinctions among the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). First, he acknowledges and internalizes what was previously taught.
"Deeply awakening to saṃsāra" means to realize that the beginning and end, arising and ceasing, and so forth, are all characteristics of saṃsāra.
"Discerning the heterodox and the orthodox" means that to use the conceptualizing mind to measure Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) is heterodox;

to enter directly into Perfect Enlightenment with a straightforward mind is orthodox. "The fearless eye of the Way" refers to the fact that fear arises from doubt; now, [one must eliminate] this doubt.
Because one has eternally severed all anxieties, one attains the fearless eye of the Way.
One who gives rise to resolute faith—meaning that with a single conviction that "mind is Buddha," there is no further doubt—can no longer be diverted by heterodox teachings.

Furthermore, such a person will no longer follow the realms of saṃsāra to give rise to various views of cyclic existence. Below follows the formal request, which consists of four parts; the first is the inquiry regarding saṃsāra.
First, regarding the root of saṃsāra: one asks what the fundamental nature of this saṃsāra is. Second, regarding the various modes of grasping and rejecting:
one asks how many distinct natures of saṃsāra there are. Third, regarding the different natures of saṃsāra:
one asks how many levels of distinction there are in cultivating the Bodhi of the Buddha. Fourth, regarding the attainment of Bodhi: once Bodhi has been attained...
How many kinds of skillful means should one employ to turn the mind back [from samsara] and enter it in order to deliver those within samsara?
These matters are all of the utmost urgency for practicing the bodhisattva path in the final age. Therefore, I pray that you will not abandon great compassion and clarify these matters.
If one’s mind is not disturbed by the cycle of samsara and one’s views are not defiled by samsara, then the eye of wisdom will be purified and awakening realized.
The mind is like a mirror; its radiance shines everywhere, enabling one to perfectly realize the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, right knowledge and vision.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

O son of good family, you are truly able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous [teachings]."

The meaning thereof is to cause all bodhisattvas to purify their eyes of wisdom, and to cause all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, awaken to the true mark of reality, and attain the patience of non-arising. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received these instructions, rejoiced; together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
Why is the root of saṃsāra called the profound, secret, and subtle meaning?
It is because the true nature of ignorance is itself buddha-nature. If one can thoroughly comprehend the true nature of ignorance, one will thereby comprehend the tathatā-buddha-nature.
This is because the tathāgatagarbha is identical to the ālayavijñāna; it is through inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation.
Because it is not known through discursive thought, it is said that this Dharma is extremely profound and subtle, and few are able to believe in it.
Furthermore, it is said that even non-regressive bodhisattvas cannot know it.
Since bodhisattvas do not know it, and only the Tathāgata can know it, it is called "profoundly secret. It is also called the "subtle and wondrous meaning. If one knows this meaning...

Thus, one will not be obstructed by the cataracts of illusion; with the eye of wisdom purified and clear, one will forever sever fundamental ignorance, penetrate deeply into the true mark of all phenomena, and be able to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Good son, all sentient beings have been in saṃsāra since beginningless time due to various forms of affectionate attachment and craving.

Therefore, this Tathāgata, while residing in a pure land, teaches the Dharma regarding defiled lands; thus, he directly points to the moisture of the heart of love that nourishes rebirth as [the cause]."
This is the root of saṃsāra within the three realms; this answers the first question.

It means that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the three realms give rise to craving through their deep gratitude and heavy attachment toward their parents, wives, and children, as well as through their firm, sticky clinging.
For this reason, parents and descendants are born in succession without interruption, and thus there is saṃsāra. Worldly people are unable to bear this burden.
This is a matter of great significance. Having become deluded and turned one's back on the nature of awakening, though one possesses the body of a man, one lacks the resolve of a true hero.
Merely because the root of craving is impure, one is entirely bound by the threads of desire; thus, through birth after birth and death after death, there is no way to escape.

For this reason, Ānanda took the occasion of his own defilement to trigger the profound unfolding of the Great Teaching. As Confucius also said: [The Master said, "I have heard that in the past, when Yao was about to abdicate the throne to Shun, he first tested him by placing him in a situation of extreme danger."]
"The thorn desires; how could it possess rigidity? Thus one knows that the cycle of rebirth within the three realms has only craving as its root and nothing else.
Whether among all the various species in the worlds—born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation—all arise because of lustful desire.

To rectify one’s nature and destiny, one must know that saṃsāra has craving as its root. Because various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Desire arises from craving; life exists because of desire. Sentient beings cherish their lives, yet this still relies upon the foundation of desire.
With craving and desire as the cause and the cherishing of life as the effect, one gives rise to various states of aversion and compliance toward the objects of desire.
When the mind turns away from objects of desire and gives rise to hatred and envy, one creates various karmas; for this reason, one is reborn again in the hells or as a hungry ghost.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, and having become weary of the path of karma, one abandons evil and delights in good, thus manifesting again as a deva or human.

Furthermore, knowing that all forms of craving are to be loathed and detested, one discards craving and delights in renunciation, yet returns to nourish the root of craving, thereby manifesting again the superior fruits of conditioned existence.

Because they all remain within saṃsāra, they do not achieve the Noble Path. Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and be freed from all cycles of rebirth, they must first sever greedy desire and eliminate craving.
Good son, when a Bodhisattva manifests transformations in the world, it is not with craving as the basis;
rather, through compassion, he causes others to relinquish their attachment, and by means of [manifesting] greedy desires, he enters into saṃsāra. If...
All sentient beings of the final age who are able to renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, and forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra,
diligently seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, will immediately attain awakening within their pure minds.
This answers the second question regarding how many types of natures exist within the various realms of saṃsāra. The egg-born arise from thought; the womb-born arise from emotion;
the moisture-born are produced by contact; and the transformation-born respond to separation.

Although these differing modes of birth have distinct natures that vary from one another, these four modes of birth encompass all natures throughout the three realms; therefore, it is said that they comprise "all natures."
All take lustful desire as the cause for forming the very nature of birth and death; they also take lustful desire as the cause for forming the very life-force of birth and death.
One should know that the saṃsāra of the three realms has only craving as its root.
This is because from the moment sentient beings emerge from the mother’s womb, the nature of craving arises simultaneously with them; thus, there is this nature of craving.

It serves as the primary cause. Moreover, there are further various objects of the five sensory realms—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—which act as auxiliary causes to assist in the arousal of the nature of craving.
It is like fire that, upon encountering wind, causes its flames to blaze even more fiercely.
By this, one creates various evil karmas; by this, one undergoes various retributions. Even through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these cannot be obstructed or severed.
Furthermore, it is not only after birth that the nature of craving arises simultaneously [with the body];
even at the very moment of initial conception, one develops attachment toward the parents due to greed and craving. Thereafter, one stirs the mind of desire and...
There is sexual desire; thus, desire arises from craving. Furthermore, it is through sexual desire that one subsequently conceives the notion of entering a womb within one's parents.

It is within this very notion that life is transmitted; therefore, life exists because of desire. Thus, we know that sentient beings' attachment to life is established by depending upon the root of desire.
This is because their past craving and desire serve as the causal condition for its manifestation. And so...

Present craving for life is the fruit produced by past karma. Since there is now this craving for life as a fruit, one further encounters the various objects of the five sensory realms in the present;
toward those that accord with one's desires, attachment arises, and toward those that oppose one's desires, aversion arises, giving rise to delusion and clinging.
Once delusion and clinging have arisen toward these two types of objects—those favorable and those unfavorable—one further creates all manner of evil karma.
Due to these present causes of affliction, karma, and suffering, one further invites the severe retribution of the three miserable realms in the future.
Thus, it is clear that the karmic retributions of the three miserable realms all have craving and desire as their root.

Once one knows that the severe retributions of the three miserable realms reside in craving and desire, one develops a profound sense of revulsion toward those objects of desire and seeks liberation from them; therefore, one loves wholesome karma and detests [unwholesome] desire.
Evil karma. One then abandons evil karma and cultivates wholesome karma. Evil refers to sexual misconduct and the like, while wholesome refers to abstaining from sexual misconduct and so forth.
Because this wholesome karma serves as the cause for rebirth among humans and devas of the desire realm, the fruit of rebirth among humans and devas of the desire realm subsequently manifests.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Though the form moves outward, the mind..."
Their traces still intersect. From this point downward, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, knowing that one is weary of the Desire Realm yet craves the First Dhyāna, one abandons the Desire Realm and enters the First Dhyāna. Becoming weary of the First Dhyāna yet craving the Second Dhyāna, one then abandons the First Dhyāna and enters the Second Dhyāna.
Becoming weary of the Second Dhyāna yet craving the Third Dhyāna, one then abandons the Second Dhyāna.
He enters the third dhyāna. Becoming weary of the third dhyāna and longing for the fourth, he again abandons the third dhyāna and enters the fourth.
Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, he realizes that the various states of joy and weariness in the three preceding heavens are nothing but attachments to superior pleasures;
that they are all merely objects of craving and thus fit only for loathing. Therefore, he discards that craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Not...

The mind that knows joy and equanimity is, in fact, craving; it returns to nourish the very root of craving. Because of this cause of immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*), one consequently experiences the superior, conditioned fruit of goodness.
Thus, although one enters the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) which are none other than joy and equanimity, these are collectively termed "subduing craving.

Yet, because the root of craving has not been exhausted, all such states remain within saṃsāra and do not constitute the fruit of sainthood (*ārya-phala*). Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* says:

Although this is not yet the unconditioned, truly immovable stage (*aniñjya-bhūmi*), because the application of effort based on the attainment of something has reached maturity, one knows that all types of natures within the three realms have craving as their root.

Therefore, those sentient beings who wish to exit the three realms, transcend birth and death, and escape the cycle of saṃsāra must certainly first sever the root of desire and eliminate the thirst of craving. To penetrate...
This very point constitutes the Arhat who has transcended the mundane world. A question is asked:

"If Bodhisattvas do not sever their craving and enter into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to extensively perform Buddha-works, for what reason must they instead study the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) to sever craving, eliminate thirst and attachment, and seek liberation from birth and death?
The answer is: When Bodhisattvas enter *saṃsāra* to deliver sentient beings, it is entirely by means of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
The manifestation of a body in the world is like a flower in a mirror, or the moon reflected in water; it is not as if sentient beings truly possess this body because of lustful desire as its cause.
Rather, by the power of great compassion and the power of great vows, [the Buddha] manifests in the same activities to gather [beings], causing them to abandon their attachment.
He provisionally enters birth and death through the gate of craving and love, yet in reality, he possesses no root of attachment whatsoever.
If one is oneself possessed of craving and thus falls into birth and death, how could one possibly sever the craving of others and cause them to transcend birth and death?

Therefore, practitioners in the末法 (mofa) age, if they can externally renounce the five sensory objects of desire and internally eliminate the two minds of aversion and attachment, will forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra and attain a pure mind. With this pure mind, they should diligently seek [the Way].
The realm of Perfect Enlightenment can be realized through the pure mind; it is just as gold extracted from ore is fit to be fashioned into vessels.
If it were merely quicksilver or gold-mercury, it would flow away upon entering the furnace.
In that case, one could not even escape saṃsāra, so how could one hope to attain enlightenment? It would be impossible.
"Good son, all sentient beings, due to fundamental craving, give rise to ignorance, which manifests as the five distinct natures that are unequal.

These appear with varying degrees of depth and shallowness based on two kinds of obstructions. What are these two obstructions? First, the obstruction of principle, which hinders right knowledge and vision;
second, the obstruction of phenomena, which continues the cycle of birth and death. What are the five natures? Good son, if this..."
As long as the two obstacles have not been severed and extinguished, one is said not to have attained Buddhahood.

If sentient beings forever abandon craving and desire, they first eliminate the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), yet if they have not yet severed the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), they can only realize and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they are unable to manifest and abide in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
Good son, if all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment...
"O Samudra, you should first make a vow to diligently sever the two obstacles. Once these two obstacles are subdued, you will be able to awaken to and enter the realm of a Bodhisattva.

If the obstacles of phenomena and principle are forever severed and extinguished, you will then enter the subtle and wondrous Perfect Enlightenment of a Tathāgata, the fulfillment of Bodhi, and Great Nirvāṇa.
Good son, all sentient beings realize Perfect Enlightenment; it is only when they encounter a virtuous friend [that they manifest it]."
Based on those practices for the causal stage, at that time of cultivation there are both sudden and gradual approaches.
If one encounters the path of the supreme bodhi of the Tathāgata, regardless of whether one's faculties are great or small, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
If sentient beings, though seeking virtuous friends, encounter those with false views and fail to attain correct awakening, this is termed the lineage of external paths.
The errors and faults of false teachers are not the fault of sentient beings. This is called the fivefold differentiation of the natures of sentient beings.
This answers the third question regarding how many kinds of distinctions there are in the cultivation of the Bodhi of the Buddha.
All sentient beings take craving as their root, which nourishes ignorance, causing that ignorance to manifest, spread, and proliferate.

Like creeping vines clinging to branches, each is bound by fetters; thus, within the state of *tathatā* (suchness), which is equal and without differentiation, the distinctions of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are manifested.

That these all appear with varying degrees of depth and shallowness due to the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) means that, when comparing ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), the obstacles of ordinary beings are deep while those of the Two Vehicles are shallow.
When comparing the followers of the Two Vehicles to Bodhisattvas, the obstacles of the Two Vehicles...
The hindrances for Bodhisattvas are deep, while those for Śrāvakas are shallow. If a Bodhisattva stands in contrast to a Buddha, the Bodhisattva possesses hindrances whereas the Buddha has none.
What are these two hindrances? The first is the hindrance to principle (*tattvāvaraṇa*), also called the hindrance to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Because one does not penetrate the meaning of the single dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*) and the mind is in disharmony with it, thoughts suddenly arise; this obstructs the principle that is to be known and hinders the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is what is named [the first hindrance].
It acts as an obstruction; this is ignorance (*avidyā*). Second is the obstruction of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), also called the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*).

This refers to how turbid and vexing dharmas disturb the mind, such that one fails to understand phenomena, giving rise to delusion and creating karma. Because the succession of birth and death continues without freedom, it is termed an "obstruction";
this refers to the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*). What are the five natures? First, it is said:

Those in whom both obstacles remain and have not yet been eliminated are the most profound; they are called "not yet having attained Buddhahood" and are also termed "the nature of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanatva*).

This refers to those within the three realms, among the six paths of humans and devas. Although their karma differs as good or evil, because the root of craving has not been severed, they all remain in saṃsāra and do not achieve the fruit of sainthood.

"Two" refers to those who have permanently abandoned sensual desire but, having only severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*), lack the power to eliminate [the remaining obstacles] simultaneously.
Those who sever the cognitive obstacles but directly transcend the three realms without regarding sentient beings can only realize and enter the minor fruits of the two vehicles;
they remain outside the gate, dwelling in a thatched hut, and have not yet clearly established themselves within the realm of a bodhisattva.
These obstacles are shallow compared to those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet deep compared to those of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-śukla-pakṣa*).

Therefore, sentient beings in the final age who wish to float upon the Tathāgata’s great ocean of Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vajra-cakra-bodhi*) should first give rise to the great vow in order to sever these two obstacles.
Regarding the third point, "both obstacles are simultaneously suppressed and one is able to awaken to and enter the bodhisattva realm":

this refers to those who cultivate the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and, by relying on the nature and characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*), attain profound faith and understanding; they enter the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

Furthermore, they cultivate the Mahāyāna factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which gradually suppress and eliminate the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) and the grasped object (*grāhya*), thereby inducing true vision (*tattvadarśana*); these are called [the factors conducive to penetration].

Regarding the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): because one merely abides in the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇa*) and has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] grounds, this obstacle is shallower than those of the two vehicles, yet deeper than that of entering the grounds.
If the two obstacles are severed in part, one enters the first ground; if the two obstacles are completely severed, [one attains full realization].
One immediately enters the subtle, wondrous, and perfect awakening of the Tathāgata, abiding in unsurpassed, perfect bodhi.

With the perfect clarity that has emerged from obstructions, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s great nirvāṇa and is able to transform sentient beings until the end of the future. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The ten kinds of obstructions are: first, the obstruction of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which refers to those [afflictions] arising from conceptualization within the two obstructions. Based on...

Because those seeds establish the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), the two vehicles, upon the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), sever only one type [of seed] and are thus said to have attained the nature of an Arya.
When Bodhisattvas first reach the path of seeing, they sever both types and are thus said to have attained the stage of an Arya.

Second is the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the threefold karma of error and transgression arising therefrom. These obstruct the two...
The extremely pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the first stage can permanently sever the third obscuration of dullness and ignorance.
This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes the loss of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.

That obscuration impedes the sublime meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage, as well as the three types of superior wisdom (*prajñā*) they produce. Upon entering the third stage, one can permanently sever it.
[The fourth is] the abandonment of the obstacle consisting in the manifestation of subtle afflictions.

This refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), comprised of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the sixth consciousness. That obstacle obstructs the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the fourth stage;

upon entering the fourth stage, one is able to abandon it forever. The fifth is the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the lower vehicles. This refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration...
[This] causes [beings] to weary of birth and death and aspire to enter nirvāṇa, similar to the two lower vehicles’ aversion to suffering and longing for cessation.
That [obstruction] hinders the path of non-differentiation in the fifth bhūmi; upon entering the fifth bhūmi, it can be permanently severed.

The sixth is the obstruction of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics, which refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that clings to the active manifestation of coarse characteristics regarding defilement and purity. That [obstruction] hinders...
The sixth stage is the path of non-defilement and non-purity; upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to permanently sever it.

The seventh is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle marks, which refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that involves the manifestation of subtle marks grasping at arising and ceasing.
This obstructs the sublime path of signlessness in the seventh stage; upon entering the seventh stage, one is able to permanently sever it. The eighth is [the obstacle] within signlessness...

It acts as an obstacle to the preparatory application (*prayoga*). That is to say, it is a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents the signless contemplation (*animittadhyāna*) from arising spontaneously.
Upon entering the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to sever it forever. Because it is severed forever, one attains two masteries (*vaśitā*).

Ninth is the obstacle to the unwillingness to act for the benefit of others; that is to say, it is a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions which [prevents] one from [engaging in] the benefit and happiness [of others].
Sentient beings do not wish to apply themselves with diligence; they seek only to cultivate their own benefit.

These constitute obstacles to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage, which can be permanently severed upon entering that stage. Once these obstacles are severed, one attains the four analytical knowledges.
Tenth is the obstacle of not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena, namely a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which prevents [mastery] over all phenomena.

One attains mastery. At the time of entering the tenth stage, one is able to permanently sever those obstacles to the great wisdom of the Dharma-cloud stage and the activities arising from its contained treasury, and performs great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Although one has attained mastery over phenomena in this stage, there remain residual obstacles that have not yet been called "ultimate," namely: the innate, subtle cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and...

There are seeds of spontaneous afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, these are all severed instantaneously, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.

Therefore it is said: "The two obstructions of conceptualization are absent in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*); those associated with the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are eliminated in each successive stage;

the seeds and manifestations of the seventh are eliminated through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and after the diamond path, they are entirely non-existent. An objection is raised: "All..."
If all sentient beings equally realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), why are there distinctions among the five natures? Answer:

Although sentient beings alike realize the nature of perfect enlightenment, this depends on the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) they encounter—whether they belong to the Mahāyāna, the Hīnayāna, or the vehicle of humans and devas—which differ from one another. Each [sentient being] then takes what they themselves have realized and attained...

Thus, those who hear the Dharma follow the habitual tendencies of their conditioning. Depending on the practice of the causal-ground dharmas they perform, there arise differences between the sudden and the gradual approaches.

If they encounter a great spiritual friend (mahā-kalyāṇamitra) who shows them the path of correct cultivation for unsurpassed bodhi, enabling them to partake in the equal flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, then [the distinction between sudden and gradual] is no longer relevant.
Both large roots and small roots all attain the fruit of Buddhahood; thus we know that their nature is fundamentally one.

It is through the influence of conditioning (*vāsanā*) that they become fivefold, not because there are five natures by essence. As for these five, although sentient beings seek virtuous friends, they may encounter false teachers.
Lacking the eye of right view, their minds were unable to discern it;

they followed the causal practices performed by those [heretics], such as the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika practices of smearing ashes and plucking out hair. Though they practiced with diligent hardship, they did not attain right awakening and thus entered the lineage of external paths.
They claimed, "My own eyes are fundamentally correct because my teacher was a true teacher," yet this error lies with the false teacher.
This is not the fault of sentient beings. These distinctions of the five natures arise entirely from the depth or shallowness of their two hindrances.
Good son, Bodhisattvas enter all worlds solely through the skillful means of great compassion to awaken those who have not yet realized the truth;
they even manifest various forms and appearances, as well as conditions of both adversity and favor, working alongside others to transform them and lead them to Buddhahood. All of this...

Relying on the power of pure vows from time immemorial, if all sentient beings of the final age should give rise to a superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should make the pure great vows of a Bodhisattva, speaking thus:

"May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and seek out spiritual friends; may I not encounter externalists or those of the two vehicles. Relying on these vows, I shall practice gradually..."
All obstacles are severed; when obstacles are exhausted and vows fulfilled, one ascends the pure Dharma-palace of liberation and realizes the wondrously adorned realm of Great Perfect Enlightenment.
This answers the fourth question: how many kinds of skillful means should be employed to deliver sentient beings by returning to the midst of worldly afflictions? Therefore—
The answer was: "Exclusively by means of the single supreme skillful means of great compassion, one enters into all worlds to awaken those who have not yet realized the truth.

Even to the point of manifesting forms according to the various classes of beings—whether as enemies or as kin—one employs the practice of 'sameness of purpose' (sāṃbhoga) to gather and transform them, leading them to Buddhahood."
All of this is sustained by the power of pure vows made during past causes; therefore, one is able to view all things with equal vision through a single eye.
Were it otherwise, it would become the great compassion of attachment and views.

Thus, sentient beings of the final age who give rise to a superior and resolute mind, desiring to traverse the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment, should make a great vow: "May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment."

Seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Do not encounter non-Buddhists (tīrthika) or those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), for the views of non-Buddhists are deviant and the scope of the Lesser Vehicle is narrow.
Relying on this power of aspiration, diligently sever the two obstacles (āvaraṇa). Because the obstacles are exhausted, everything encountered will be nothing other than liberation.

Because his vows are fulfilled, there is nothing in the objective realm that is not Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). In this way, the three virtues are perfectly luminous and the three bodies (*trikāya*) are simultaneously realized.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses: "Maitreya, you should know: all..."
All sentient beings fail to attain great liberation; they all fall into the cycle of birth and death because of craving and desire.
If one can sever both hatred and love, as well as greed, anger, and delusion, one will attain the Buddha-way through no distinction of nature. The two obstacles will be forever extinguished;
by seeking a teacher, one attains right awakening, accords with the vows of the Bodhisattvas, and relies upon Great Nirvana throughout the ten directions.
All Bodhisattvas, through the power of their great compassionate vows, manifest entry into the cycle of birth and death.
Those who practice now and sentient beings of the final age should diligently sever all attachments and views; they will then return to Great Perfect Enlightenment.
That all sentient beings fail to attain liberation is entirely due to being bound by craving within birth and death, preventing them from escaping.

If one can sever hatred and attachment, eliminate the three poisons, and no longer rely on the fivefold differentiated natures as the practice of the causal ground, but instead rely upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating, pure awakening, all shall attain the Buddha-way. Therefore:

Regarding "all shall attain Buddhahood": because they have severed the two obstacles, sought authentic awakening, and given rise to great vows, they are able to take the ocean of Great Nirvana as their support and abide in the Perfect Enlightenment of a Buddha. As for why one must necessarily give rise to vows:

it is because the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all sever craving and views through the power of their great compassionate vows and enter the cycle of birth and death; therefore, the present Bodhisattvas...
When one severs craving and views, one shall immediately enter Great Perfect Enlightenment.
*The Near Commentary on the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Definitive Meaning*, Fascicle Three;
*The Near Commentary on the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Definitive Meaning*, Fascicle Four.
Expounded by Shi Tongrun of Er Leng’an.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sake..."
To speak of such inconceivable matters as these— things never before seen and never before heard— we who are now graced by the Buddha’s skillful guidance find our bodies and minds at peace,
having attained great benefit. We pray that you will once again proclaim for all the assembled Dharma-multitude the perfect enlightened nature of the Dharma King,
as it is known to all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, and the World-Honored Tathāgatas.

"What is the distinction regarding the realization of what has been attained? May sentient beings of the final age, upon hearing this holy teaching, attain awakening in accordance with it and be able to enter [the path] through gradual stages.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made his request three times, beginning again and again.

Although the five natures have been clarified and their gradations distinguished, if one regards these five natures as being real, then one will be muddled regarding True Suchness and wisdom will not be pure.
Therefore, he poses a question according to the capacity of the listener to clarify that all five natures arise from a single nature;
it is because their subduing, severing, cultivation, and realization differ individually that distinctions exist. First, he acknowledges what was previously stated.
Regarding "matters that are inconceivable" and so forth: this means that both the causes and effects of defilement and purity are all transformed through the permeation of inconceivable karmic power;
therefore, they cannot be perceived or seen. Consequently, even though the World-Honored One usually does not easily expound them, they are likewise difficult to hear.
Now, having received the World-Honored One’s patient and skillful guidance, we have been able to hear this Dharma; thus, both body and mind are at peace.
This is most profound. The interlocutor below requests clarification:

"I understand that although the distinctions among the five natures are established based on the depth or shallowness of the two hindrances, the nature of awakening is perfect and complete, universally realized by all sentient beings as fundamentally non-dual.
If this is so, then what the ordinary person, the non-Buddhist, the follower of the Two Vehicles, the Bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata realize and attain should not be different. Why is this?"
Yet there are five distinct natures. If one understands this meaning, one will be able to accord with the nature of awakening and gradually enter it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O son of good family, you..."
"You are indeed able to inquire of the Tathāgata on behalf of sentient beings in the final age regarding the distinctions between the gradual and sudden approaches.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

Regarding the distinction of gradual progression: this refers to the fact that by severing the ten types of afflictions, one realizes the ten types of suchness, each with its own particular distinction.
Thus, while the five natures exhibit distinctions, that which is realized likewise exhibits distinctions. The preceding chapter treated the matter in terms of the severance of afflictions.
This chapter concerns the realization of truth.
Good son, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a nature that exists as a nature; it arises in accordance with all natures, yet is without grasping and without realization.
Within the true mark (*dharmatā*), there are in reality no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings. Why is this? Because both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are...
It is an illusion; because illusion is extinguished, there is no one who attains realization. It is like the faculty of the eye, which cannot see itself.
Its nature is inherently equal, yet there is no one who is equal. Sentient beings are deluded and inverted, unable to eliminate all illusions;

thus, within the false exertion of what is extinguished and what is not yet extinguished, distinctions appear. If one attains the Tathāgata’s quiescence and accords with reality, there is truly nothing.

"Quiescence and that which is quiescent" refers to the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Because it does not possess the five natures, it is called "the existence of the nature of non-nature.

Since Perfect Enlightenment does not abide in its own nature but arises in accordance with all natures, when these natures arise, they immediately accord with the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment.
Since arising is truly without intrinsic nature, there are no illusory phenomena grasped by sentient beings, nor is there any dharma of quiescence realized by Bodhisattvas.

If one speaks according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) from the perspective of the second gate, then distinctions may exist between the grasper and the grasped, or the realizer and the realized.
However, if one speaks according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) regarding the true mark, there are truly no such things.
Sentient beings are the grasper, while Bodhisattvas are the realizer. Why is this?
Because both sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are relative phenomena, all of which are illusory defilements. Once these illusory defilements are removed, everything is awakened.
How, then, could one again perceive those as sentient beings who are graspers or as Bodhisattvas who are realizers? It is, for example, like the visual faculty.
One does not perceive one's own eyes, because the awakened nature (bodhicitta) realized therein is fundamentally equal; thus, one does not perceive a person who can bring about this equality.
It is known that the originally existing awakened nature is perfectly complete in both sentient beings and Buddhas, and in reality, there is no distinction between them.
Nevertheless, as for the appearance of differences, it is because sentient beings dwell within states of delusion and inverted views;
unable to suddenly extinguish all illusory transformations, they gradually sever and gradually realize according to the depth or shallowness of their intellectual power.
Within this process of false effort, the designations of the five natures (pañca-gotra) are manifested. If one realizes the tranquility of the Tathāgata’s body and mind...

In the stage of non-duality that accords with the fundamental limit of the equality of cessation, one does not perceive even the slightest dharma that is extinguished, nor does one perceive a person who can bring about extinction; how, then, could there be any distinction between the five natures?

Good son, all sentient beings since beginningless time, due to their deluded conceptions of a self and their attachment to what they love as "mine," have never known for themselves that [their minds] arise and perish from moment to moment.
Consequently, they give rise to hatred and love, becoming addicted to and attached to the five desires.

If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment and clarifies the process of arising and ceasing, they will immediately realize that the nature of this birth is inherently one of weary toil.
What is meant by "differences being manifested within false effort" refers to the fact that all sentient beings,

due to the self-clinging of the *manas-vijñāna* (seventh consciousness) and the conceptual clinging to a self by the *mano-vijñāna* (sixth consciousness), grasp at both self and phenomena through these two consciousnesses.
Consequently, they falsely identify the four great elements as their own physical body and the reflected images of the six sense-objects as their own mind.
They have never known that their own thoughts arise and perish from moment to moment; thus they give rise to hatred and attachment.

Becoming addicted to and unable to relinquish the objects of the five sensory realms, they give rise to the five desires, and consequently there is the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.

If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the pure, perfect *bodhi* nature—which is the dharma of quiescent extinction—and further elucidates for them the nature of thought...

To contemplate arising and ceasing is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Upon hearing this teaching, they realize that these worldly afflictions and discursive thoughts are all their own deluded and chaotic imaginings;
yet, they have not yet been able to subdue or sever the two attachments, nor have they been able to accord with the nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
Although they are called "awakened," it is actually non-awakening; therefore, they are said not to have attained Buddhahood. Furthermore—
This is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Furthermore, if there is someone who has forever severed all toil and anxiety and attained the purity of the *dharmadhātu*, yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to themselves, they will lack mastery over Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). This is called an ordinary person conforming to the nature of enlightenment.

If one cultivates *śamatha* and severs the two delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thereby permanently eliminating the obstacles of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), one can then internally give rise to tranquil pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
At that time, one attains directionless purity; hence it is said: "When weariness and deliberation are forever severed, one attains the purity of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi*).
"Weariness and deliberation" refers to the mental deliberations of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). Because one severs such weariness and deliberation, one attains the pure Dharma.
Having done so, one then clings to this pure understanding, which in turn becomes an obstruction and a hindrance for oneself.
Consequently, one fails to attain mastery over the perfect enlightened nature. Thus, the former masters said: "The divine light is not obscured;

it is a glorious legacy for all ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor cognitive understanding. This is because to maintain cognitive understanding is called the Two Vehicles' compliance with the enlightened nature. For...

However, merely severing the attachment to a self is called "semblance awakening. One refers to them as "ordinary beings" rather than "followers of the Two Vehicles" because, since their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been eliminated, they are the same as ordinary beings.

A former master said: "Even when one reaches the Dharma-body, because attachment to phenomena has not been forgotten and one's own views still persist, falling into the side of the Dharma-body is also a sickness. He also said: "One rides a donkey and does not see the carp."
This is a sickness. To refuse to dismount from one’s donkey is also a sickness. The former sickness is that which ordinary beings suffer;
the latter sickness is that which those of the two vehicles suffer.
Good son, all bodhisattvas take views as an obstruction. Although they sever the obstruction of views, they still abide in the awakening of views. Awakening...
To be obstructed by obstructions and lack self-mastery—this is called a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi) following along with the nature of awakening.
This clarifies that for a bodhisattva, one who perceives attainment and guards pure understanding constitutes an obstruction.

For the sake of sentient beings, they diligently seek liberation by cultivating various kinds of sublime provisions; thus, they sever the obstructions of understanding and do not abide in a state of pure objects. And...
Because they have not yet realized the emptiness of the grasper and the grasped, they dwell predominantly in the external gate while practicing the bodhisattva path;

thus, they have not yet subdued or extinguished the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) induced by these two types of grasping. Consequently, they are unable to prevent the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of those two graspings from arising, and they still perceive a "perceiver" who is aware.
Thus, they abide in the perception of this awareness; yet this very perception of awareness remains an obstacle—namely, the "gnat."
Although the cicada has shed its shell, it still clings to the cold branch; thus, within Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*), it does not attain mastery.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "To posit a slight object before oneself and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, this is not truly abiding in consciousness-only.
This refers to the Bodhisattva in the stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*) who accords with the nature of awakening, yet because they have not yet severed the [notions of] dharmas...
Grasping is also called "semblance-awakening.
Good son, having illumination and having awakening are both termed obstructions. Therefore, the Bodhisattva dwells constantly in awakening without abiding;
illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescent extinction. It is like a person who cuts off their own head; since the head is already severed, there is no...

As for "one who is able to sever": by means of an obstructing mind, one causes all obstructions to cease of themselves. Once obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no longer any one who obstructs or is extinguished.
The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
All the various verbal teachings of the Tathāgatas that reveal the path to Bodhisattvas are likewise so. This is called the Bodhisattva having already...
Those who have entered the stages (bhūmi) accord with the nature of awakening.
This means that although Bodhisattvas in the stage of the Three Worthies (trividha-ārya) cultivate samādhi, there still remains the wisdom that illuminates and the principle that is realized;
thus, the characteristics of subject and object, as well as the states of being able and unable to forget these, persist. For this reason, both are termed obstacles. Therefore...

By practicing *dhyāna*, one cuts off illuminating cognition (*āloka-jñāna*). When both illumination and cognition are severed, subject and object are both forgotten, and one enters into the *dharmatā*.
Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata and exhausts the realm of the Buddhas; one partially realizes the equal *dharmakāya* and first ascends to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Thus, one attains constant awakening that does not abide, for the illuminator and the illuminated are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-kārikā* says: "If..."

At that time, with respect to the object of focus, wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended. At that moment, one abides in *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), because one is free from the characteristics of the two grasps (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

By means of the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) employed in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one severs the conceptual attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) and realizes the universally pervasive *tathatā* (suchness).
One no longer grasps at the various signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); wisdom and suchness are equal and identical. It is like a person who [severs] themselves...

Regarding its "head": because the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has been severed, one no longer perceives a wisdom capable of severing it—just as, once the head is severed, one no longer perceives a person capable of severing it.
This conversely reveals that prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), all [practitioners] used an obstructed mind to extinguish obstructions;
thus, there were delusions to be suppressed and persons who could suppress them. Consequently, the illumination and the illuminator were simultaneously extinguished at the first stage.

The above constitutes the severing of the conceptual attachment to dharmas and the realization of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). It is not severed by means of severance, nor realized by means of realization.

It is not like those prior to the [first] stage who, with an obstructed mind, seek to extinguish obstructions; therefore, they do not perceive any obstruction to be extinguished, nor the wisdom that extinguishes such obstructions.
Thus it is said: "Obstructions have already been severed and extinguished, yet there is no one who extinguishes obstructions. Why is this? Because of the stage...

The aforementioned bodhisattvas all practiced by recognizing the six perfections as phenomena taught by the *nirmāṇakāya* buddhas; they had not yet reached the realization that the essence of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment) is inherently complete with all practices.
This is like failing to see the true moon and instead grasping at the finger pointing toward it as the moon itself.

Upon reaching the stage of *prayoga* (preparatory application), one investigates names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions; however, it is only upon reaching the first bhūmi (*prathamā-bhūmi*) that names and meanings finally become empty, and [delusions] are severed.
Cease speech and thought; practice the six pāramitās purely through wisdom without giving rise to grasping or attachment. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the dāna-pāramitā and the others in accordance with it."

Just as one sees the moon but does not mistake it for the pointing finger, from this point the Bodhisattva attains the true Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and enters the stage of penetration (*prativedhāvasthā*).

This is called "one who has already entered the stages" (*bhūmipraviṣṭa*), following in accordance with the nature of awakening (*bodhisaṃtati*). Because they have partially severed the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and partially realized ultimate truth, this is termed "partial awakening" (*pradeśabodha*).
"Good son, all obstacles are ultimate awakening. Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation.

Whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all called nirvana. Wisdom and folly are both universally termed prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are equally bodhi.
Ignorance and suchness are no different realms. All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms..."
Lust, anger, and ignorance are all the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). Sentient beings and their lands share the same single Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands. Those with nature and those without nature equally achieve the Buddha-way. All afflictions (*kleśa*) are ultimately liberated.

The ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) illuminates and understands all phenomena as being like empty space. This is called the Tathāgata’s accordant awakening to the nature of reality.
The Treatise says: "As when the stages of a Bodhisattva are fully perfected through skillful means, in a single thought-moment of correspondence, one awakens to the initial arising of the mind;
yet the mind has no mark of beginning. Because of being far removed from subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind, and the mind is then eternally abiding."
Therefore, one sees that all afflictions, ignorance, and obstructive dharmas are of one identical, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening.
Because one has not yet seen original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), there is gain and loss;

once original awakening is seen, it is fundamentally without loss and now without gain. Thus, every dharma is true, and there is nothing that is not liberation. At the time when one has not yet awakened—
This means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have formation and disintegration, whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) have neither formation nor disintegration.
Once awakening has occurred, that which is conditioned is itself the unconditioned, and that which is unconditioned is itself the conditioned;
thus, both the phenomenon of formation and the phenomenon of destruction are *nirvāṇa*. Prior to awakening, ignorance and wisdom were certainly two distinct dharmas. Once awakening has occurred—
Subsequently, the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; therefore, both wisdom and folly are termed *prajñā*.
Before awakening, false dharmas and correct dharmas are utterly distinct; once awakened, they are the equal primordial limit.
Therefore, for both Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists, this is equally bodhi. Prior to awakening, ignorance and true suchness (tathatā) were originally two distinct dharmas;
once awakened, the limit of ignorance is itself the limit of true suchness, and thus there is no separate object.
Prior to awakening, the three trainings and the three poisons are correlative dharmas; once awakened, the three poisons...
These are precisely the three trainings; therefore, both constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Before awakening, sentient and insentient beings stand as opposing adversaries;
once awakening is attained, heaven and earth share a common root and all phenomena are one body.
Thus, sentient beings and their environments are of one single *dharmatā*. Prior to awakening, the two realms of suffering and pleasure appear clearly distinct.
Once awakened, suffering and pleasure are fundamentally empty; thus, both the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands.
Before awakening, there were distinctions among the five natures; once awakened, these five natures are originally one single nature, and the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle.
Therefore, those of the three vehicles who possess the nature for enlightenment and even the icchantikas who lack it all attain the Buddha-way. Not yet...
Before awakening, there is duality between bondage and liberation; once awakened, one knows that the very place of bondage is liberation and the very place of liberation is bondage.
Therefore, afflictions are themselves liberation. Before awakening, one gives rise to emotional attachments toward objects;
once awakened, one discerns all phenomena without giving rise to conceptual discrimination. Thus, by means of the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, [one realizes this].
He illuminates all phenomena as being like empty space. Therefore it is said: "Those who are free from the marks of thought are equal to the realm of empty space;
the single mark of the dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-body. This is called the Tathāgata’s accordant pure awakening.

The severance of ignorance characterized by the appearance of arising is called ultimate awakening. The above has demonstrated the gradual severance and gradual realization from the stage of an ordinary person up to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Good son, all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should, at all times, not give rise to deluded thoughts.

They do not suppress or extinguish their deluded thoughts; they abide within the realm of delusive perceptions without applying further discernment, and in this lack of discernment, they do not distinguish what is real.
When those sentient beings hear this Dharma-gate, they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, without giving rise to alarm or fear.
This is what is called conforming to the nature of awakening.

Good sons, you should know that such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as to great Bodhisattvas, thereby planting the roots of all virtues.
The Buddha said that such a person is called one who has accomplished all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This specifically cites the dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment to show practitioners what they should cultivate.

One who gives rise to deluded thoughts at all times—this "arising" is itself the illness, the mad mind, and the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). If one does not give rise [to them] at all times...
Delusive thoughts—by means of them, one transcends the state of an ordinary being and enters the nature of awakening. Thus, the ancient masters said: "Do not engage in false imaginings.

Those who weary themselves of toil and deliberation to extinguish the deluded mind—this extinction is itself a sickness; such people are madmen, they are those who drive a boat by pulling at a fixed stake, and they belong to the stage of the Two Vehicles.
One who does not even attempt to extinguish or suppress these various deluded minds transcends the Two Vehicles and enters the nature of awakening.
To dwell within the realm of delusive thoughts and apply augmented cognition while remaining therein is to see what is already awakened. This "augmentation" is itself a sickness;
it is a deranged mind, like placing a head upon a head. This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*trīṇi śaikṣāṇi*).

To dwell within delusive thoughts without applying augmented cognition is to transcend the Three Stages of Worthiness and enter the nature of awakening. Regarding the phrase "discerning the reality within non-cognition," this "discernment" is itself a sickness.
This mad mind is the opening of the mouth that forms a pair of stakes; it is the Bodhisattva on the ground.

Without cognitive understanding and without discriminating the real, one immediately transcends the ten stages and enters the nature of awakening. If the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.

The four illnesses are suddenly eliminated and the four madnesses are suddenly stilled. This stilling is itself Bodhi; this is the capacity of those with the faculty for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
This is also the method for practicing the Dharma-gate. Therefore, the former masters said: "The moment the mind is directed toward it, worldly afflictions fill the eyes;
if the mind does not direct itself toward it, every thing is truly authentic, every thing is luminous and wondrous.

If those sentient beings were to hear this Dharma, they would give rise to deep faith and resolve, certainly upholding it without ever forgetting or losing it. Furthermore, they would not give rise to alarm or fear, but would directly and immediately accept it.
This is precisely what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.

Those such as Sudhana, the dragon girl, the woman with a broad forehead, and the butcher, who attained the fruit of kalpas of cultivation in a single lifetime, are of this same class. Therefore, it is praised, saying:
"These sentient beings did not plant roots of goodness under one, two, three, or four Buddhas; they have previously [done so] under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."

Only those who have planted roots of goodness under all Buddhas are able to shoulder this task. The Buddha says that when such a person first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, they immediately attain perfect awakening.

They realize that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind; they achieve the body of wisdom, not through the awakening of another, and are thus said to have accomplished the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Pure Wisdom, you should know: The nature of perfect enlightenment is without grasping and without realization; there is neither bodhisattva nor sentient being. Whether in the state of awakening or non-awakening, there are gradual differences.

Sentient beings are hindered by their own delusions; bodhisattvas have not yet transcended the notion of awakening. Upon entering the stages, they abide in eternal quiescence and do not dwell [in the realm of signs]."
All marks are fully perfected by the Great Awakened One; this is called "universal compliance.

If sentient beings in the final age do not give rise to delusions in their minds, the Buddha says that such people are Bodhisattvas in the present life. Their merit in making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is already complete.
Although there are many skillful means, they are all termed "wisdom of compliance."
It is said that in the perfectly awakened nature (*bodhicitta*), there is no differentiation of what is realized, nor is there any gradual sequence of realization;
rather, there is only a gradual differentiation between awakening and non-awakening.

Therefore, those who attain the purity of the *dharmadhātu* yet maintain a pure understanding that still harbors obstacles are the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Those who have removed the obstacle of conceptual understanding yet still maintain the perception of awakening—

The three levels of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) are as follows: those who have departed from illumination and awakening to realize quiescent extinction are those who have "ascended the stages" (*bhūmi-praviṣṭa*).
Those who reach the perfection of the nature of awakening such that there is nothing they do not accord with are the Greatly Awakened (*mahābuddha*).

If one does not give rise to mental movement or discursive thought in any place whatsoever, this is called the perfection of merit; in the present life, one becomes a second Teacher. Although the above are thus divided...
Regarding the two gates of sudden and gradual, insofar as they accord with pure awakening, there is in truth no difference between them.
That is to say, while the skillful means are manifold, the wisdom that accords with them is one.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have extensively analyzed for us such accordance with the nature of awakening, enabling all bodhisattvas to perceive the luminosity of the awakened mind. We now receive this through the Buddha’s perfect voice."
"World-Honored One, one does not attain wholesome benefit merely through cultivation. World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates;
those who come from various directions do so by more than one path. All Bodhisattvas' adornment of Buddha-lands and their attainment of Bodhi are not achieved by a single expedient means.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim for us all the expedient means, the gradual stages, and the cultivation thereof."

"How many types of practitioners are there in total? May the bodhisattvas of this assembly and those sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) era who seek the Mahāyāna quickly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself, casting his body to the ground.
Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.
The chapter on Maitreya clarifies the afflictions to be abandoned; the chapter on Pure Wisdom clarifies the principle to be realized.

If the contemplative practices to be cultivated were not clarified, there would be no way to abandon the afflictions and realize the truth, and one’s majestic power would not attain sovereignty. Therefore, the following is clarified.
The wisdom of contemplation thus cultivated possesses such majestic power that it prompts [the Buddha] to issue inquiries according to the capacity of the disciple.

"The luminosity of the awakened mind" means that when obscurations are exhausted, the awakened mind becomes clear and pure. "Receiving the Buddha’s perfect voice," and so forth, refers to internalizing the principle of the sudden realization through the forgetting of the mind;
realizing that the mind does not give rise to delusions is precisely what is called the accomplishment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is not dependent on...
If one attains such excellent benefit through practice, how much more so for those who practice with diligent application? The World-Honored One’s response below is a formal request.

The "great city" is a metaphor for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*); that there are four gates, each of which can be entered, is a metaphor for the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) of Perfect Enlightenment, as each contemplation provides a path of access.
"All expedient means and gradual stages" refers to the inquiry regarding the practices to be cultivated, as well as—

The "practitioner" refers to one who cultivates contemplation. If one understands these two kinds [of practice], one will swiftly attain awakening and be able to sport within the great ocean of profound quiescence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
O sons of good family, it is well that you are able to ask the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age."

"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Īśvaradhipateya, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Good son, the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades all the ten directions. It gives birth to the Tathāgatas and is of one essence and equal to all phenomena.
Regarding all practices, there is truly no duality; yet the skillful means that accord with them are immeasurable in number.
When fully encompassing that which is returned to, according to the distinctions of their inherent natures, there are three kinds.
The unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment flows forth as all Tathāgatas of the ten directions; therefore, it is identical in essence and equal to all Buddhas.
Furthermore, it flows forth as all defiled and pure phenomena; therefore, it is again identical in essence and equal to all phenomena.
Although all practitioners may manifest myriad practices in their quest for the truth, there is nothing that is not ultimately the One Way.

Yet, because sentient beings differ in their faculties—whether sharp or dull—and in the density or thinness of their afflictions, as well as in their states of mental sinking or agitation, they employ expedient means to provide teachings according to these conditions in infinite numbers.
If one summarizes and encompasses where all these paths lead, they are all able to accord with the nature of awakening; yet, [they differ]...
There are, in brief, three other expedient methods of contemplative practice that encompass all such practices without exception.

Good son, if a bodhisattva, having awakened to pure, perfect enlightenment, takes stillness as their practice with a mind of pure awakening, they will clarify all discursive thoughts and perceive the restless agitation of consciousness.
