As tranquil wisdom arises, the adventitious dust of body and mind is forever extinguished. Thereupon—
One is able to internally generate tranquility and pliancy.
Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas in the worlds of the ten directions appear therein like reflections in a mirror. This skillful means is called *śamatha*.

"Awakening" (wu) refers to understanding and realization; it means "to employ. "Taking" (qu) means first realizing that within one's own body there exists the nature of pure, perfect, and unchanging *bodhi*.
Because of the habit of distraction, one has never been aware that every thought-moment is subject to arising and ceasing.

Therefore, one employs this pure awakening to take stillness as its practice in order to cause all discursive thoughts to subside. Thus, the confusion of the discriminating consciousness is perceived.

The agitation is like that of a boiling cauldron, yet as tranquil wisdom gradually arises, the former false identifications with the physical body—the transient guest—and the dust of shifting conditioned reflections, all cease to arise.
One is then able to inwardly give rise to stillness and pliancy;
because dullness has been removed, the body is light, and because excitement has been removed, the mind is at peace. By means of this...
Because it is quiescent, all the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of the Tathāgatas appear within it, just as reflections appear in a clear mirror.
This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Such a skillful means is called *śamatha*.

*Śamatha* is here translated as "calming" (*zhi*), for it can calm all weariness and discursive thought. If this contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is perfected, one is then able to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), realize the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and enter the stage of abiding in faith (*śraddhādhimukti*).

"Good son, if Bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they use their mind of pure awakening to realize that the nature of the mind, as well as the sense faculties and their objects, are all produced by illusion.
They then give rise to various illusions to eliminate the illusionist, and transform these illusions to open the way for the illusory multitude.
Because they give rise to these illusions, they are able to inwardly manifest great compassion and ease. All Bodhisattvas, from [this point]..."

This arising practice gradually progresses and increases. Because the observer of the illusion is not identical to the illusion, and because all that is not the observation of the illusion is itself an illusion, one becomes eternally detached from illusory appearances.
This perfected and wondrous practice of the Bodhisattvas is like a sprout growing from the soil;
this skillful means is called *samāpatti*.
The mind, sense-faculties, objects, and realms constitute the eighteen *dhātus*. All arise from the delusion regarding reality caused by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
They originally possess no self-nature and are entirely produced through the transformations of illusory persons.

This is because fundamental ignorance arises in opposition to reality, and the eighteen realms, in turn, arise from that ignorance; thus, the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness is that which is conjured by illusion.
As for the fundamental ignorance and the karmic consciousness that constitute the illusionist, one gives rise to illusory wisdom to eliminate this illusionist.
Furthermore, one manifests various dependently originated phenomena that are like illusions to guide sentient beings who are likewise like illusions.
Because they engage in illusory practices, they are able to internally give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Since their compassionate resolve to deliver sentient beings is so urgent and their great compassion is so superior, their vigor and diligence are such that even if they lacked a physical body, their mind and body would still be pliant.
All Bodhisattvas who initiate practice from this point on—meaning that there are no practitioners of the Bodhisattva path who do not proceed from tranquility (*śamatha*)—[proceed in this manner].
Within the awakened mind, various illusory activities arise and gradually progress, such as the three provisions (*sambhāra*) and the four applications (*prayoga*).
Regarding the statement that "the one who contemplates the illusion is not the same as the illusion":

although the illusion itself is ignorance, the one who observes it as being an illusion is wisdom (*jñāna*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*), and thus is not the same as the illusion. This is because wisdom and consciousness are not the same.
This is why it is so. As for the statement that "not all contemplations of illusion are themselves illusions":
if one investigates this thoroughly, it is not only that which is illusory that is an illusion; even the wisdom that contemplates the illusion is likewise an illusion.

This is because within the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), there is no room to establish even the subject who contemplates the illusion, let alone the wisdom that contemplates the illusion. Therefore, one first comes to know the illusion.
The subject gives rise to illusion; next, one uses illusory wisdom to eliminate the subject; finally, one uses the awakened mind to sweep away illusory wisdom.
Only when both wisdom and consciousness are forgotten and both subject and object are extinguished does one attain permanent detachment from illusory appearances and enter the First Ground.
This is called the wondrous and perfect preparatory practice (*prayoga*) cultivated by a bodhisattva. Regarding the analogy of soil producing sprouts:
the soil is a metaphor for the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) of the causal stage; the sprouts are a metaphor for illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*).

This means that one gives rise to illusory wisdom based upon pure awakening, and enters the awakened mind through illusory wisdom. This is termed the practice of "conforming to reality" (*jñatattvānugata*). This skillful means is called *samāpatti*. III.

*Samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium" (*dengzhi*). Because within *samādhi* one is able to reach the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), if this contemplation is perfected, one subdues the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), realizes a semblance of awakening, and enters the stages of the three worthies (*tri-paṇḍita*) and four applications (*catuḥ-prayoga*).
Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they employ this mind of pure awakening to neither grasp at illusory transformations nor at various states of stillness.
They clearly understand that both body and mind are hindrances; their non-conceptualizing, luminous awareness does not rely on any such obstructions.

Thus, they forever transcend the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction. While experiencing the world and its bodies and minds within the sphere of sensory dust, they remain like [a lotus in water].

Just as the sound of metal clashing within a vessel resonates outward, so too do affliction and nirvana no longer obstruct one another. One is then able to internally give rise to tranquil extinction and light ease (*praśrabdhi*).
This wondrous awakening accords with the realm of tranquil extinction, a state that neither self nor others, nor body nor mind, can reach.
The lives and lifespans of sentient beings are all but floating thoughts. This skillful means is called *dhyāna*.
"Not grasping at illusory transformations or the mark of stillness" means that one does not grasp at either of the two dharmas of prior śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One directly observes that the awakened mind is unmoving, knowing it clearly and constantly, without giving rise to discrimination;
this is as described in the Mañjuśrī Chapter. Because one understands that both body and mind are hindrances, one does not grasp at illusory transformations.
Furthermore, because one realizes that non-cognitive luminosity does not depend on any impediments, one does not grasp at the mark of stillness.
One is aware throughout the day yet never truly aware; one is luminous throughout the day yet never truly luminous—this is non-cognitive luminosity.

Since body and mind are of the nature of dependence upon others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while non-cognitive luminosity is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one directly contemplates the nature of awareness.
Such a person forever transcends both obstructed and unobstructed realms; that is to say, they sever both extremes and emerge far beyond the middle. Baizhang said:
"The numinous light shines alone, utterly detached from the sense faculties and their objects. Its essence reveals true permanence, unconstrained by words and letters.
The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. Simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. This...
This is precisely the Tathāgata-dhyāna and the Patriarchal-dhyāna. Regarding those who experience the world and possess bodies and minds within the realm of sensory dust:
once they have entered this gate, in their daily activities there is no need to apply the mind. It is simply eating when hungry and sleeping when tired;
nurturing the "sacred embryo" by the waterside and beneath the forest trees. Though their form dwells amidst the mundane, [the mind remains detached].
Though confined within boundaries, there is not a trace of worldly sentiment. This is what is meant by "though the spirit transcends the world, it remains perpetually within the realm.
It is like the resonance of a bell within a vessel that issues forth beyond it—"hāng" (鐄) refers to the sound of a large bell.
A common proverb says, "The bell is inside the temple, but the sound is outside," which captures the sense of being unimpeded. This arises because one does not grasp at dualistic appearances.
Yet, emerging alone, one thoroughly understands that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; thus, they do not obstruct or hinder one another.

One is then able to internally give rise to the light ease of quiescent extinction (*śānti*). As for "quiescent extinction": it is "quiescent" because one does not grasp at stillness, and "extinguished" because one does not grasp at illusions.
Since not even a speck of dust can be established, body and mind are light and at ease. This is what is meant by: "When arising and ceasing have both ceased, [quiescence...]"
This refers to the manifestation of cessation (*nirodha*). This realm of quiescent extinction can only be accorded with by the wondrously enlightened true mind;
if the four marks (*catur-nimitta*) persist, one cannot accord with it. Therefore, that which accords with the wondrous enlightenment is beyond the reach of one's own or another's body and mind.
"Self" refers to the mark of selfhood (*ātma-nimitta*); "other" refers to the mark of personhood (*pudgala-nimitta*). Thus speaks of this realm of quiescent extinction.
It is not something that can be reached by those who possess the marks of a self or a person, nor can it be attained by those who possess the marks of a sentient being or a life-span.

Because Bodhisattvas on the [first] ground have severed the dualistic attachments to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-dvaya-grāha*) through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it cannot be reached by those who have realized [the fruits of] self and person.
Because they have severed the innate (*sahaja*) dualistic attachments to a self and phenomena, [it is beyond] sentient beings and life-spans.
To eliminate discursive thoughts, this skillful means is called *dhyāna*. *Dhyāna* is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*jing-lü*).
It refers to contemplating while remaining calm, and remaining calm while contemplating; it is the general designation for the equilibrium of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

If this contemplation is perfected, one severs ignorance and realizes partial awakening (*anupūrva-bodhi*). This is what is cultivated from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, good son, these three Dharma-gates are all in close proximity to and in accord with Perfect Enlightenment. It is because of them that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained Buddhahood;
and the various skillful means, as well as all similarities and differences, of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all rely upon these three.
Various types of activities. If one attains perfect realization, it becomes Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
Good son, suppose there were someone who cultivates the noble path and brings to fruition the fruits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas;
this would not equal the merit of someone who, upon hearing this unimpeded Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment, practices in accordance with it for even a single kṣaṇa.
These three types of contemplative practice above are all skillful means for drawing near to and accords with [the goal];
they are what are called the "Dharma-practice of the causal stage. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions relied upon these as their cause to achieve perfect enlightenment.

All the various and distinct skillful means cultivated by those of the Three Grades of Sages and the Ten Stages of Bodhisattvas are likewise cultivated based on these three types; thus, they are identical skillful means.
This refers to Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*), who have first attained the noble nature (*ārya-dhātu*) and realized the dharma of equality.
"Alternative means" (*anya-upāya*) refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the stages, who have not yet realized the noble nature and remain within the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If one relies solely on the initial contemplation, severing the grasping at a self and realizing a semblance of awakening, this is the means for the two vehicles to accord with the nature of awakening.
Those who practice the second contemplation simultaneously subdue the two attachments to self and phenomena, thereby realizing the semblance-enlightenment;

this is the expedient means for the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness (śaikṣa) to accord with the nature of enlightenment. Those who practice the third contemplation simultaneously sever the two attachments to self and phenomena, thereby realizing the partial enlightenment;
this is the bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (bhūmi) acceding to the nature of enlightenment. If these three contemplations proceed gradually...

Advancing further, at the final moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one suddenly severs the ignorance of the phase of arising through adamantine wisdom and enters ultimate enlightenment.
Therefore it is said: "If one attains perfect realization, one immediately becomes Perfect Enlightenment. The passage beginning with "Good son" below cites the inferior to manifest the superior.
According to the teachings, it is stated that if even one or two people are encouraged to uphold the five precepts or the ten precepts, they shall attain [the result].

The merit is already immense; how much more so when one causes so many people to achieve the state of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), forever transcending the three realms and the ten entanglements (*daśasaṃyojana*). Yet this does not equal that of someone who practices *Perfect Enlightenment* (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) for even a single moment.
How much less so for one who practices the sublime contemplation perfectly over a long period? Thus, Guifeng said: "Hearing the Five..."
This is called the supreme field of merit for the gift of jewels; the meaning of half a verse is superior to the teachings of the Hinayana that outnumber the sands of the Ganges.
Truly, it is because there is no dharma that is not upheld and no capacity that is not reached.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse: "O Mahātejas, you should know:
the mind of the Unsurpassed Great Enlightenment is fundamentally without dual characteristics at its ultimate limit. Yet, in accordance with various skillful means, their number is immeasurable.
The Tathāgata has summarized and revealed them as being of three kinds: Śamatha, which is tranquil, is like a mirror reflecting all images; it is like an illusion."
Samādhi is like a sprout gradually growing; dhyāna is solely quiescence, like the clapper within a bell. These three sublime gateways to the Dharma all accord with awakening.
It is by means of these that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas attain the realization of the Way.
Because these three matters are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate nirvāṇa.
These three types of contemplation are practiced gradually when entered in successive order, and practiced suddenly when entered by leaping over the stages.
*Dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is precisely the gateway for sudden practice.
