In the fifth fascicle of the *Brief Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Dafangguang Yuanjue Xiduo Luoyi Jing Jineshi),
composed by the Venerable Tongrun of Er Leng-an: At this point,
the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇa rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, such a Dharma-gate is truly rare.
World-Honored One, regarding these various skillful means, how many ways of cultivation are there for all Bodhisattvas within the gate of Perfect Enlightenment?"
“I pray that you will provide a skillful exposition for the sake of this great assembly and for sentient beings of the future age, so that they may awaken to the true mark of reality.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made his request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
The characteristics of the three contemplations previously explained were clear;

however, it remains uncertain whether the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas at various stages involve one person possessing all three, or three persons each possessing one, or whether they occur sequentially, simultaneously, in regular order, or by skipping stages.
Therefore, Bodhisattva Bianyin (Vibhūṣaṇa) asked a question according to the capacity of the audience regarding how many types of cultivation there are. This is clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

The "Twenty-five Perfect Penetrations" clarify twenty-five kinds of wheels (*cakra*). Although their skillful means (*upāya*) differ, they all converge in *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment).
Therefore, it is said: "Skillful means are revealed and taught so that one may awaken to the true nature (*tathatā*)."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇasvara, saying: “Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

That you are able, for the sake of this great assembly and for the sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Then the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇasvara, receiving these instructions with joy, along with the entire great assembly, remained silent.
Nevertheless, listen, son of good family.
In the perfect enlightenment and purity of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no cultivation nor any cultivator.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age practice based on the power of illusion due to their lack of awakening; at that time, [the distinction between subject and object] arises.
The twenty-five kinds of the wheel of pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-samādhi-cakra*).
"Wheel" (*cakra*) has the meaning of "turning," for all bodhisattvas turn this wheel to reach the stage of a Tathāgata.
"Wheel" also has the meaning of "crushing," for all bodhisattvas turn this wheel to crush the obstacles of affliction and grind away ignorance.
Initially, there are three wheels for practicing the three contemplations individually; next, there are twenty-one wheels for practicing the three contemplations alternately;
finally, there is one wheel for practicing the three contemplations perfectly. These comprise twenty-five wheels in total.
These twenty-five wheels also involve gradual cultivation and realization within the realm of deluded effort—both conscious and unconscious—and thus possess distinctions. The following text...
The twenty-five contemplations of the wheels are all based on Guifeng’s *Brief Commentary*.
If bodhisattvas focus solely on extreme tranquility, through the power of that tranquility they will permanently sever the afflictions and achieve ultimate perfection.
Without rising from his seat, he entered parinirvāṇa. This bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha alone.
If, however, these bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, they manifest various transformations and activities within the world through the power of the Buddha.
He fully practices the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva; regarding dhāraṇīs, he does not lose his tranquil mindfulness or various still wisdoms.
This bodhisattva is said to practice samāpatti exclusively.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions, do not engage in activity, and exclusively sever the afflictions,
such that when the afflictions are completely severed they realize the true reality, these bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* alone.

First, the single cultivation of the three contemplations is explained. First is the contemplation that clarifies the turbid and ceases activity: by means of the power of stillness, one cuts off afflictions and realizes *nirvāṇa*.
Although this is the practice of a bodhisattva, its conduct is no different from that of the two vehicles; it is called the single cultivation of *śamatha*.
Second is the observation of Cook Ding wielding his blade at will.

Because he has realized that all phenomena are like illusions, he is able to manifest various functions through the power of the Buddha and fully practice pure and wondrous conduct, as described in the "Ten Practices" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Although he performs the myriad practices, he does not lose the characteristics of cessation (*śamatha*) and tranquil wisdom (*vipaśyanā*); this is called practicing samāpatti in isolation.

Ti. Third, the sound of "Cheng" (Present) issues forth the contemplation of non-obstruction. Not grasping at functional activity while alone severing afflictions is still the activity of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
When afflictions are completely severed, one then realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*); this is the activity of a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*).
There are two kinds of afflictions, namely those within the realm (*adhātuka*) and those outside the realm. Severing only those outside the realm is the activity of the two vehicles. Together with...
To sever that which is within the realm [of delusion] is the activity of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva first attains profound stillness and, with a mind of tranquil wisdom, illuminates all illusions, they then initiate bodhisattva practice therein.
Such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of tranquility, they thereby sever the afflictions and transcend birth and death forever.
Such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings,
and subsequently sever afflictions to enter into nirvana, such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced śamatha,
then cultivated samāpatti, and finally practiced dhyāna.
If bodhisattvas, having severed afflictions through the power of ultimate stillness,
subsequently initiate the pure and wondrous practices of a bodhisattva to deliver all sentient beings, such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, then cultivated *dhyāna*,
and finally cultivated *samāpatti*.
If Bodhisattvas, by the power of ultimate stillness, sever the afflictions with their minds, and further deliver sentient beings while establishing worlds,
these Bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and then cultivated *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* in equal measure.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate tranquility, first give rise to transformations and subsequently sever the afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha and samāpatti together first, and cultivate dhyāna afterward.
If bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness to support their quiescence, and subsequently initiate activity to transform worlds,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha and dhyāna together first, and then cultivate samāpatti.

The first seven wheels take the attainment of stillness as their primary function, while simultaneously combining the illusory and the tranquil to form seven stages, thereby clarifying that there is no provisional, no middle, and nothing that is not empty.
First is the Contemplation of the Ferry Crossing to Rescue All: practicing meditative concentration to transcend the mundane is the ferry;
developing wisdom to transform sentient beings is the act of rescuing all. Second is the Contemplation of the Tranquil Sea and Clear Sky: when the sea is tranquil, the waves...
1. The Waves Do Not Move: When the sky is clear, the nature of water is transparent and bright. 2. The Three-Headed, Three-Eyed Contemplation:
Practicing all three contemplations together is like having three eyes. 3. The Simultaneous Cultivation of the Three Dots: The three dots are the letter *i* in the Sanskrit script;

when one person cultivates these three types together, it is called "simultaneous," which does not mean they occur at the exact same moment. 4. The Single and Double Contemplation of the Five-Syllable Seed-Mantra: First, practice them individually.
Next, practicing both [meditations] together is like the character "you" (猶). Therefore, they are called "single and double. Sixth is the meditation on the single-legged, double-headed [creature].
In the *Bai Ze Tu* (White Deer Diagram), there is a mountain spirit whose head is like a drum and has two faces visible from both front and back, yet it has only one leg.

Practicing the two meditations together is like having two heads; practicing one meditation alone is like having only one leg. Seventh is the meditation on the falling fruit and blooming flowers. This means:

By means of the tree of tranquil concentration, one binds the fruit of nirvana; once the fruit has fallen, one further delivers sentient beings through the contemplation of illusion, like the blossoming of flowers.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, adapt themselves in various ways to attain ultimate stillness, such a bodhisattva—
This is called first practicing *samāpatti* and subsequently practicing *śamatha*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, attain quiescence through various objective realms,
such a bodhisattva is said to first practice *samāpatti* and subsequently practice *dhyāna*.
If bodhisattvas perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abiding in tranquility while severing afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then cultivated *śamatha*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions and abide in ultimate tranquility,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then cultivated *dhyāna*, and finally cultivated *śamatha*.
If bodhisattvas, through the skillful application of the power of transformation, reach both quiescence and cessation while remaining in accord with them,
such bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated samāpatti and then practiced śamatha and dhyāna in tandem.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, employ various functions to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever the afflictions,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice samāpatti and śamatha in parallel, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna.
If bodhisattvas support their state of quiescence through the power of transformation and subsequently abide in pure,
effortless meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such bodhisattvas are said to practice *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of *śamatha*.

Next, the seven wheels begin with illusion (*māyā*) and combine it with tranquility (*śānti*) to form seven alternating stages, clarifying that there is nothing empty, nothing central, and nothing not dependent upon conditions.
First is the contemplation of "Arms followed by Civil Virtue," like King Wu casting down his armor and weapons to forge agricultural tools after his conquest of Zhou.
Second is the contemplation of "Resigning from Office upon Accomplishing Merit": the development of wisdom to benefit sentient beings is called "accomplishing merit. Having practiced...
1. The contemplation of retiring from office through internal tranquility. 2. The contemplation of the illusionist’s mastery of arts:

first arising transformations to perform magical feats, and subsequently returning to the tranquil essence—this is the mastery of the arts. 3. The contemplation of the divine dragon hidden in the ocean:

arising illusions to save sentient beings like a divine dragon scattering rain, and returning to the essence to enter stillness like hiding in the ocean. 4. The contemplation of Nāgārjuna’s penetration of the truth: first arising illusions... [text fragment]

Later, he returned to stillness and tranquility. This is like Nāgārjuna, who initially practiced illusory arts to extensively convert those on heterodox paths, but later cultivated the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*) and personally attained the fruit of sainthood.
Regarding Śāṇavāsa’s manifestation of signs: Śāṇavāsa was the teacher of Upagupta.
First, he used his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to manifest signs and subdue the arrogance of Upagupta’s disciples; subsequently, he entered [the womb].
He will surely return to quiescence. Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata first transformed sentient beings and subsequently returned to quiescence.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to supreme stillness and abide in purity, such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated śamatha.
If bodhisattvas initiate activity through the power of quiescence, such that their functioning accords with quiescence regarding all objects,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced dhyāna and subsequently practiced samāpatti.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, employ various intrinsic natures to abide in meditative concentration and give rise to transformations,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* within the practice of *dhyāna*, and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to functional activity through the unconditioned nature of things,

and their purified objects of perception return to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* within *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation and various forms of purity, abide in dhyāna and give rise to emanations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated dhyāna and practiced śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure.
If bodhisattvas, supported by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), give rise to transformations from ultimate stillness,
these bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* and *śamatha* simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of *samāpatti*.
If bodhisattvas employ the power of quiescence to support their transformative manifestations, thereby giving rise to the wisdom of a supremely tranquil,
pure, and luminous state, such bodhisattvas are said to practice dhyāna and samāpatti simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of śamatha.

These seven wheels take stillness (*śānti*) as the primary focus, while initially incorporating both tranquility (*praśama*) and illusion (*māyā*), thus forming seven through their mutual interaction.

This is because clarity is neither empty, nor false, nor not-central. First is the contemplation of the ocean of emptiness of precious clarity: stillness is like precious clarity; tranquility is like the ocean of emptiness. Second is the contemplation of the wondrous function of space:
the essence of stillness is like space; illusory transformation is like its function. Third is the manifestation of *śūnyatā* (the ether-being).
1. The Contemplation of the Divine Spirit (Śūnyatā-deva): When the Śūnyatā-deva encounters the Buddha’s radiance, he briefly manifests;

thus, there is first quiescence, then stillness, and finally the illusory manifestation. 2. The Contemplation of Kāśyapa Returning to Samādhi: First he realizes the essence, then he gives rise to supernormal powers, and finally he enters samādhi.

3. The Contemplation of Prabhūtaratna Displaying Supernormal Powers: The Buddha Prabhūtaratna first attained Buddhahood and realized the essence; subsequently, from within the stupa, he manifested great [powers].
1. The Contemplation of Sound Like Stillness and Illusion Without Obstruction: Sounds are like stillness and illusion, unimpeded. 2. The Contemplation of the Six Directions Rising as Transformations:

As one contemplates, the six directions manifest transformations; immediately, a multitude emerges from the earth, appearing from below. 3. The Contemplation of the Imperial Blue Containing Transformations: This jewel contains the images of all things;

when confronted, it transforms and responds accordingly, yet upon responding, it returns to emptiness. Just as the tranquil essence contains function, responding to conditions like an illusory arising, it then returns to stillness and tranquility. These are the twenty [contemplations].
The single wheel most clearly manifests the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unite with all things, they will not depart from the nature of enlightenment regarding any characteristics or natures.
This Bodhisattva is said to be one who practices the three kinds of self-nature purity in a perfectly integrated manner.
Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the Bodhisattva; all Bodhisattvas practice in this way.
"To perfectly unite all things with the wisdom of perfect enlightenment" reveals the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

Whether it be their nature or their characteristics, whether stillness or illusion—even down to bending, turning, looking up, looking down, spitting, scolding, playing, or laughing—all do not depart from the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment.
This is what is meant by "all obstacles are ultimate enlightenment. This is called the perfect cultivation of the three [mysteries].
Contemplation. There is nothing that does not accord with the pure self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment. "Good son," and so forth, concludes the primary cause.
If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this wheel, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and contemplate in tranquility.
Solemnly seek compassion through repentance for twenty-one days. Place a marker at each of the twenty-five wheels and, with a sincere heart, seek compassion while drawing lots as they fall.
According to the markings revealed by the draw, one will immediately know whether the path is sudden or gradual. If there is even a single moment of doubt or regret, success will not be achieved.

This section indicates the ritual procedures for the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and the skillful means of applying the mind. "Brahmacarya" refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*). "Tranquility" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Reflective thought" is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). "Observation" is wisdom (*prajñā*). "Repentance" is the disclosure of prior karmic actions.
"Each settling upon their respective markers" refers to the dedicated cultivation of a single practice. If one gains confidence in a single gateway, then...
One must perform divination. If one hesitates or cannot decide, then rely on the power of the Sage to determine what should be practiced.

One should take [the knot] as it comes to hand and not engage in selection; thus, one forms a knot according to what the hand takes. By opening and showing the knot according to what was taken, one will immediately know whether it is sudden or gradual.
Do not covet other contemplations. If even a single thought of doubt or regret persists, the mind will not be focused and the resolve will falter.
If they were not identical, they would not be accomplished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "Discerning Sound, you should know:
The unimpeded and pure wisdom of all Bodhisattvas Is born entirely from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That is to say, from *śamatha* and *samādhi*."
Ti-ch'an-na. There are twenty-five kinds of cultivation regarding these three dharmas, both sudden and gradual.

Among the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all practitioners of the three periods of time, there are none who have not attained Bodhi by means of this dharma. This excludes only those of sudden enlightenment and those whose natures do not accord with the Dharma.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should constantly uphold this wheel and accord with it.
Diligently practice; by relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, one will before long realize nirvana.
Regarding sudden and gradual cultivation: sudden cultivation refers to the final single wheel, while gradual cultivation refers to the twenty-four wheels.
This excludes only those who have attained sudden enlightenment—meaning those who do not establish stages or the conceptual characteristics of words and letters.
As previously stated, for one who does not give rise to deluded thoughts at any time, there is a single severance that is forever severed, and a single realization that is forever realized.
Those of the highest faculties transcend this by means of the method of severance, or they do not practice by relying upon it;
or those who lack the faculty of faith and are unwilling to comply also do not rely on this for their practice.

All others—the three types of worthies, the ten stages of the sages, and all practitioners of the bodhisattva path—should rely upon this wheel of Dharma and cultivate it with diligent compliance. Having cultivated it, they should further increase their efforts.
"Diligence" means to exert oneself.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, for our sake..."

Thus he extensively explained these inconceivable matters—the characteristics of the practices on the causal stages of all Tathāgatas—causing the great assembly to attain what they had never experienced before.

They beheld how the Tamer, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, underwent diligent suffering and all manner of effort, yet it all appeared as if occurring in a single thought-moment.
We Bodhisattvas were deeply moved with joy and consolation. "World-Honored One, if this awakened mind is such by its very nature..."
"It is pure. For what reason do defilements cause all sentient beings to become bewildered and fail to enter it?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively expound for us the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), so as to serve as a guiding eye for this great assembly and for sentient beings of the future age.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Thus they made their request three times, beginning again and again.

The severing of delusions has been clarified; the realization of truth has been explained; and the contemplative practice has been concluded. Thus, the two gates of perfect integration (*yuanrong*) and sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) are fully established.

However, the root of karmic activity is rooted in the four marks (*xiang*). If these four marks are not eliminated, the root of karma will remain impure, and one will be unable to enter the gate of *dhāraṇī*.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Pure of All Karmic Obstructions (*Jingzhu ye zhang pusa*) responds to this opportunity.
This is a question. Regarding the "inconceivable matter" first realized: initially, one dharma is expanded into three; next, those three dharmas are expanded into twenty-one;
finally, those twenty-one dharmas are condensed back into one.
Yet this cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination; it can only be clearly realized by those who have attained direct realization. This is precisely all-encompassing bodhi.
This is the practice of the causal stage of the Dharma cultivated by the Bodhisattva.

Now, having heard this Dharma and personally seeing that the diligent and arduous efforts cultivated by the Tathāgata throughout kalpas do not depart from the present thought-moment, we are deeply moved by joy and consolation.
[The World-Honored One] then proceeded to grant the formal request: "If this awakened mind is originally pure, then why is it that the various practitioners of the present..."
Through diligent effort, all may attain entry. For what reason, then, are they defiled, obstructed, and hindered such that those practitioners become confused and faint, unable to enter?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively awaken us to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), explaining the reasons why they cannot enter, for the sake of sentient beings in the final age.
It acts as the eye of the True Dharma, clearly indicating the path of entry so that one does not falter midway, become confused, or fail to enter.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you are truly able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means for the sake of this great assembly and for sentient beings of the future age."

"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have through deluded imagination clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
They take these four inversions to be their real self-substance. Because of this, they give rise to the two objects of aversion and attachment.

Upon this foundation of falsehood, they further cling to falsehood; these two delusions supporting one another give rise to the path of deluded karma. Because there is deluded karma, there is deluded [retribution]."
They perceive the flow of saṃsāra; those who weary of this flow falsely perceive nirvāṇa. Because of this, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
It is not that awakening rejects those capable of entering it, for there are those capable of entering who do not enter through awakening.
Therefore, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought alike result in confusion and delusion. Why is this? Because they take as their own the beginningless, primordial ignorance.
Lord, all sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom; the nature of their body and mind is entirely ignorance.
It is like a person who does not sever their own life-force. Therefore, you should know that those who love me I accord with, while those who do not accord with me I treat with hatred and resentment.
Because the heart of hatred and love nourishes ignorance, those who continue to seek the Way [are unable to attain it].
Accomplishment. First, the four characteristics are explained in general. "Delusive thought" refers specifically to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses;

because they recklessly calculate what is non-existent to be existent, it is called "clinging to existence. Regarding these four characteristics, there are two interpretations: first, clinging to mundane phenomena; second, clinging to supramundane phenomena.
Regarding the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*): first, as for the attachment to the self of worldly phenomena, this refers to grasping at one's own essence as the self.

Calculating that the self transmigrates successively through other realms of existence, one conceives of it as a "person" (*pudgala*). Calculating that the self undergoes various transformations such as prosperity and decline, or suffering and pleasure, in continuous succession, one conceives of it as a "sentient being" (*sattva*).

Calculating that the self’s single karmic retribution and life-faculty remain uninterrupted and persist, one conceives of it as a "life-sustainer" (*jīvaka*). This is precisely delusion regarding the world.

They grasp at a self within phenomena. Because sentient beings recognize these four kinds of inverted marks of self as having substantial reality, they give rise to attachment toward themselves and aversion toward others due to this grasping at a self; they love those who accord with their self.
Those who oppose me I loathe. Furthermore, the four great elements and the five aggregates are fundamentally without a self; to now grasp them as a self is already a delusion.
To further give rise to love and hatred toward this illusory essence of a self is to add delusion upon delusion and confusion within confusion.
Because these two delusions rely upon one another, false karma arises; having created false karma, there is false existence.

As for those who revolve through the cycle of birth and death as a karmic retribution, when they come to weary of birth and death and rejoice in the path of cessation, they then falsely perceive nirvana.
Because the mark of selfhood has not been eliminated and their longing and aversion are not yet exhausted, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
It is not that the mind of pure awakening rejects people and refuses to admit them; rather, it is because of the seeker’s own [deluded] pursuit of entry.
Because people do not enter by way of the path of awakening, they are unable to enter. For this reason, those who stir their thoughts fall into birth and death and thus do not enter;
those who cease their thoughts abide in nirvana and thus do not enter. Now, it is certain that those who stir their thoughts do not enter;
but for what reason do those who cease their thoughts also fail to enter? It is truly because ignorance is twofold.

There are two types: first, the root; second, the branches and leaves. Those of the Two Vehicles only sever the ignorance of the branches and leaves, yet they still have fundamental ignorance as their sovereign master.
All sentient beings are born with ignorance simultaneously upon emerging from the mother's womb;
therefore, at the moment of birth, they lack the eye of wisdom and do not know that within the four elements and the body-mind there exists Perfect Enlightenment.

In its nature, it is like a person born blind who cannot recognize the color of milk; how could such a person know that this ignorance (*avidyā*) is the very root of the birth and death of sentient beings?
Yet, practitioners are unwilling to apply themselves to cutting off their own life-root (*jīvitendriya*).
It is like a person who refuses to sever his own life, guarding and cherishing it everywhere. Therefore, you should know that for one who has love for me, I shall give [this teaching].
One follows and cherishes those who are compliant; yet when there are those who oppose me, one resists and rejects them with hatred.
Through these two minds of hatred and love, the root of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is nurtured, leading to non-awakening and lack of knowledge.

Therefore, although those of the Two Vehicles are said to have "stilled their thoughts," their ignorance remains unsevered, and darkness continues to grow and fester in secret. Thus, they seek the state of non-arising and non-ceasing by means of a mind characterized by arising and ceasing.
As for the fruit of cessation: how could one possibly seek the heavens by digging in the earth?

Furthermore, the following section provides a detailed clarification that regarding the delusion concerning supramundane dharmas and the clinging to a self, it is not only ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle who abide within the four marks;

even the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood, prior to severing the ignorance of the mark of arising, are all subsumed within these four marks. With the exception of the Buddha alone, [all others fall within them].

Since these characteristics are ultimately exhausted [in the self], the subsequent passage uses the four phases of realization, awakening, understanding, and enlightenment to demonstrate that their beginning and end are unified solely by the single character "I" (wo).
This is similar to Confucius’s notion of the "I" in the context of "the inevitable, the stubborn, and the self," which, though divided into four, also intends a single, comprehensive "I.
However, the former refers to the worldly "I," whereas the latter refers to the supramundane "I"; thus, they are not the same.
"Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings.

Good son, it is like a person whose hundred joints are in perfect harmony who suddenly forgets his own body; yet when his limbs become slack and his nourishment and care go awry, he immediately perceives the existence of a 'self' upon the slightest application of needle or moxa.
Therefore, it is through such realization and grasping that the substance of the self manifests. Good son, as for that mind..."
Even the realization of the Tathāgata’s ultimate, thorough knowledge of pure nirvāṇa is all the mark of self (*ātman*).

While the mark of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) is easy to recognize, the mark of a dharma-self (*dharma-ātman*) is difficult to recognize; therefore, it is manifested here by way of realization, awakening, and clear comprehension.
What is called the "mark of self" refers to that which is realized by the minds of sentient beings; this very realizer is itself the self.
This is the mark. It is like a person whose hundred limbs are in perfect harmony, unaware that there is a "self.

If the four limbs are either too tight or too slack, or if their nourishment and care have gone awry, then even with a slight application of needles, moxibustion, or fire, the mark of the self immediately reveals itself.
We see clearly in the world those who are limping or crippled and capable of nothing; yet when the breast within them is level and calm, the mark of the self is absent.
If one possesses ambitions—whether in literature, intellectual skill, economics, craftsmanship, or debate—one becomes rugged and uneven;
the mark of the self (*ātman*) arises and manifests. Therefore, as soon as there is any grasping at realization, one sees oneself as the subject who realizes and nirvāṇa as the object to be realized.
This is precisely how the noble ones of the four fruits eliminate the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) while manifesting the Dharma.
The mark of selfhood (*ātma-grāha*) refers precisely to this: taking that very pure understanding as an obstacle to oneself.

It does not matter whether one has merely realized a small fruit and clings to what was realized as being "self," or even if one has realized the Tathāgata’s ultimate, perfect *bodhi* and pure *nirvāṇa*, yet fails to let go of the mark of realization—this too is the mark of selfhood. For when perfect *bodhi* returns to the state of non-abiding...

Because [the self] has been attained. Question: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the noble ones of the four fruits do not form the thought, "I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna," and so forth.
Why, then, is it said here that there is a self? Answer: Those of the second and third fruits have severed the [notion of] self within the desire realm.

The four fruits [of the śramaṇa] have severed the self of the three realms; therefore, they are said to be "selfless. Yet, because there is still a nirvāṇa to be realized and the dharma-self has not yet been forgotten, it is said that they possess a self.
Good son, what is the mark of a person? It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization. Good son, there is realization...

I no longer recognize a self; that which is realized is likewise not realized by a self. Once awakened, one transcends all who claim realization, for these are entirely marks of the person (*pudgala-nimitta*).

Good son, if the mind—even up to the point of perfectly realizing *nirvāṇa*—still regards itself as a self, or if the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening while claiming to have fully exhausted the principles of realization, it is all termed the mark of the person.

What is called the mark of a person (pudgala-nimitta) refers to when sentient beings take that which is realized through mental awakening to be non-existent, yet they themselves claim, "I am the one who can realize this non-existence. This is precisely the mark of a person.

For a Bodhisattva, having resolved to attain enlightenment, does not seek to cross over first while others remain uncrossed, but is instead urgent in saving others; thus, seeing those who do not recognize their own selfhood, he explains it as follows: "Because..."
Previously, one took that which was realized as the self; now, having awakened to its unreality, one no longer realizes it as such, and the mind no longer recognizes it as the self.
Not knowing that this awakening to "non-self" is itself the mark of a person (pudgala-nimitta)—and that this mark of a person is also the very self—is [the error].
This is because one has realized that one is capable of surpassing all those who have attained realization.

This is precisely the manifestation of the mark of self (*ātman*) by one who, while practicing the six perfections during the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*), transforms various illusions to open the way for illusory multitudes;
it is what is meant by "although the obstacles of understanding have been severed, one still dwells in views and cognitions. It is not merely that one has realized one's own capacity to transcend.
To practice the transcendence of saving sentient beings while surpassing all those who have attained realization is the mark of the human self.
Even if one’s mind reaches the point of fully awakening to the pure nirvana of the Tathāgata—the very state of realization—it is still the mark of the self.

If one allows even a single thought of an awakening mind to persist, claiming "I am able to fully exhaust the principle of realization" and asserting that there is nothing further to be realized, this is to depart from the mind of realization and yet remain within it.
Awakening—all these are termed marks of the person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Therefore, the former masters said: "Even if you have a wondrous awakening, you must spit it out.
Good son, what is the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*)? It refers to that which the minds of all sentient beings cannot personally realize or awaken to.
"Good son, it is like a person who says, 'I am a sentient being. One should know that when such a person speaks of a 'sentient being,' it is neither the self nor another.
Why is it not the self? Because if 'I am a sentient being,' then it is not the self. Why is it not another?
Because 'I am a sentient being' does not mean it is the self of another. Good son, it is only by means of the realization and testimony of all sentient beings [that this is known]."
To realize that all things are "self" and "person," yet to maintain a sense of realization regarding that which is beyond the reach of the marks of self and person—

this is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). As for what is termed the mark of a sentient being, it refers to various beings who perceive themselves as surpassing the aforementioned realization.
Awakening. That which is beyond the reach of realization is precisely the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*). It is like a person who says, "I am a sentient being";
one knows that the person speaking of a "sentient being" is certainly neither the self nor the other.
The reason it is certainly not the self is that if "I am a sentient being," then one knows it is not [the self].
I say that it is not "that" because this "I" is a sentient being and yet is not the "I" of that [self].

This is precisely the mark of self (*ātman*) that manifests when a Bodhisattva on the Grounds realizes *nirvāṇa*. It is not like the Hīnayāna, which possesses a mind of realization through the unilateral severance of self-clinging;
therefore, it is called "not-self. Nor is it like the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*), who simultaneously suppress both [extremes].
Because one clings [to experience] while possessing a mind of awakening, it is said that "it is neither that nor me.

Since one has severed both dualistic attachments to the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), one can discern that the prior realization was the mark of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), and further discern that the act of awakening was the mark of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, one can set aside the mind of realization and wash away the traces of awakening, not planting one's roots in the place of realization or awakening, nor claiming "self" or "person" for oneself.

It does not reach it. However, when one’s constant awareness does not abide in the existence of that which is understood, this very mind of understanding is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Good son, what is the mark of life-span (*āyus-lakṣaṇa*)? It refers to that which is understood by the clear and pure illumination of the minds of all sentient beings.
All karma is invisible to the wisdom that perceives it, just as the life-faculty is. Good son, if the mind perceives all states of awakening, they are all merely dust and defilement;
for that which awakens and that which is awakened do not transcend the realm of dust. It is like hot water melting ice:
there is no separate ice that knows the ice has melted. To maintain a self and awaken to a self is likewise so.

What is called the mark of a self (ātmagrāha) refers to this Bodhisattva who, having attained the pure mark of awakening through the perfect illumination of the awakened mind, merely maintains a single thought that what was previously understood is false;

yet, not having reached the state of neither attainment nor awakening, this very state of awakening is termed the mark of life-span (jīvita-nimitta). This mark is extremely subtle, extending from humans and devas up to the [Arhats].
Those whose karmic characteristics have not yet been emptied and whose karmic consciousness does not cease to function cannot perceive it.

Only those who are free from thought, whose minds are like space, and who are devoid of initial characteristics can perceive it. This is precisely the fundamental ignorance of the arising-characteristic (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).
Just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), though not perceived by itself, maintains the physical body in an uninterrupted continuity, one should formulate the following syllogism:

The characteristic of lifespan is the subject (*dharmin*). It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that it is cognized by awareness. The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is not seen by any cognitive wisdom (*jñāna*).
The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like the life-faculty. This is because Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) realize, through each preceding stage, the errors of those prior to it.

Therefore, one constantly dwells in non-abiding awakening. Upon reaching Equal Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one is able to use the pure mind of awakening to illuminate and see that the constant dwelling in non-abiding awakening throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is entirely a defilement.
To merely retain the aspect of awakening that perceives awakening is itself still not free from defilement.
This is illustrated by the analogy of hot water melting ice: although the ice has melted, there is nothing else remaining.
Ice. However, one must know that the ultimate cause of the ice’s melting is the hot water. This is because ice and hot water are relative phenomena;
they are not the fundamental substance of water itself. Now, to use subsequent awakening to awaken to the error of the prior [state] is to maintain the self while awakening to the self.
The "upper self" is the subject that awakens, while the "lower self" is the object of that awakening.
This is also a dualistic awakening, for it has not yet forgotten the characteristics of awakening and is not the inherently pure essence of awakening itself.
Only when the characteristics of awakening are simultaneously eliminated is there the perfectly complete, pure characteristic of Bodhi.
Therefore, the Mañjuśrī Chapter states: "One who perceives empty space perceives but a flower in the sky."
Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks. Although they may practice the Way with diligent effort for many kalpas, it is merely called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta);
in the end, they cannot achieve any of the fruits of sainthood. For this reason, it is called the "final age of the True Dharma.
Why is this? Because they mistake all forms of self for nirvāṇa; because they regard having realizations and awakenings as "attainment. It is, for example, like...

There are those who mistake a thief for their son; they will never achieve success with their family’s wealth and treasures. Why is this? Those who possess attachment to the self also come to love *nirvāṇa*.
They take the subduing of the root of self-attachment as the mark of *nirvāṇa*. Those who harbor aversion toward the self also come to hate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Not realizing that attachment to the self is the true nature of birth-and-death, they separately hate birth-and-death; this is called not being liberated. How could this be [the way]?
They understand the Dharma but do not attain liberation. Good son, those beings of the final age who practice for Bodhi take their own slight realizations to be self-purification;
they have not yet been able to exhaust the root of the mark of self (*ātman*).
If someone else praises that dharma, they immediately feel joy and desire to deliver them; yet if someone else slanders what they have attained, they immediately give rise to anger.

"Regret! Thus one knows that the mark of self (*ātman*) is firmly grasped and maintained; it lurks within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), sporting among the sense-faculties without ever ceasing.
Good son, because those who cultivate the path do not eliminate the mark of self, they are unable to enter pure awakening."
This clarifies that if these four marks persist, the fruit of sainthood cannot be realized. Regarding the two [types of] fruits of sainthood, if discussed generally:

by severing only the attachment to a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) while not severing the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-ātman*), one realizes the fruit of the Two Vehicles. By simultaneously subduing both the attachments to self and phenomena, one realizes the fruit of the Three Stages of Worthies (*tri-kṣānti*).
By simultaneously severing the discriminative attachments to both self and phenomena, it is called "severing the mark of the person" (*pudgala-nimitta*), and one realizes the first [stage].

The fruit of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*): By severing both the innate attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), one is said to sever the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*) and realize the fruit of the eighth stage.
If one severs the ignorance of the mark of birth (*jāti-nimitta-avidyā*), it is called severing the mark of life-span (*āyuṣka-nimitta*) and realizing the fruit of *bodhi*.

If one does not understand these four marks, then even if one practices diligently for many eons, there will still be something attained; this is merely called a superior wholesome fruit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Without having emerged from the triple world, one does not achieve any of the fruits of sainthood. Therefore, even while within the Tathāgata’s True Dharma (*saddharma*), it is called the "End of the Dharma" (*paścimadharma*).

This is because during the time of the True Dharma, there are teaching, principle, practice, and realization; during the time of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), there are teaching, principle, and practice, but no realization;
whereas in the End of the Dharma, there is teaching and principle, but no practice or realization. Because they [in the latter ages] rely upon...

First, because there is no actual cultivation or realization in taking the self as *nirvāṇa*. If one were to establish a definitive argument, only Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above would constitute the fruit of sainthood;
those of the two vehicles and the three levels of worthies are all subsumed within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since they possess realization, they are termed "accomplished. This is just like mistaking a thief for one's own son while the family treasure remains [unrecognized].
How could there be any principle of accomplishment? Why is it that those who have attained realization never ultimately accomplish any of the fruits of sainthood?

It is because both bodhisattvas prior to the stages and those of the two vehicles with their minor fruits have not yet severed the selfhood of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) and all possess attachment to self (*ātma-sneha*).
Since they possess attachment to self, they also love *nirvāṇa*. This is because they merely suppress the root of attachment to self.

It is taken as the mark of *nirvāṇa*. Because one has truly never severed the root of attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), one merely enumerates the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ śaikṣāḥ*) without entering the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*);
this is not true *nirvāṇa*. Since there is love for a self, there must be hatred toward a self; since there is hatred toward a self, one must necessarily hate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Not realizing that this very attachment to dharmas is the true root of birth-and-death, one fails to sever attachment to dharmas and instead [seeks elsewhere].
They loathe birth and death; they loathe this place as a latrine and its filth. For this reason, they fail to achieve the liberation of the Dharma, yet they still claim, "I am.
How should one know that those who possess attachment to the Dharma fail to achieve the liberation of the Dharma and yet claim, "I am"?
It is said that those who practice for enlightenment merely perceive a slight degree of realization and, on their own account, consider themselves [to have attained it].

One attains purity, yet remains unaware that the root of craving lurks within. Because the craving for dharmas has not been eliminated and one has not yet emerged from birth and death, it is known that one has not attained liberation through dharmas.
Now, by what means may one verify that the mark of self-grasping exists and that liberation through dharmas has not been attained?
Suppose, furthermore, that someone were to praise the dharma they have realized; that person would then—
When a heart of affection arises, one immediately desires to deliver [others]. If, however, one slanders the Dharma they have attained, they will immediately give rise to a mind of aversion.

Thus, one knows that the mark of self (*ātman*) is firmly grasped; its seeds then lie latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), while its active manifestations (*samudācāra*) sport through the various faculties.
In this way, the arising of seeds and manifestations is never interrupted. How could this be...?
Is it not the case that one fails to recognize all [phenomena] as the self-nature of nirvāṇa? Therefore, the *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) states:

"Because one examines the internal mind by means of external objects, the grasping at a self remains firm, persisting in a latent continuity. Thus, although the armies of wisdom have been raised many times and the hosts of Māra have been repeatedly defeated,"
The capital city of Ālaya is firm and difficult to assault, governed by its sovereign; the manas serves as its constant guard, providing a strong defense.

The consciousness (manovijñāna) acts as the minister, managing both internal and external affairs, while overseeing the generals of the five sensory consciousnesses to maintain order at the gates of the six sense faculties.
Consequently, the rebel leader frequently communicates and dallies with them, constantly stealing their passwords to delude the Dharma King and repeatedly encroaching upon his borders.

They disturb the objects of my contemplation. Although externally they are timid before Prajñā, appearing like creatures that roam by day and hide by night, internally they harbor ignorance, which persists without interruption day and night.
Thus, those practitioners of the Way cannot enter pure awakening because they have not eliminated the mark of self;
it is not that awakening rejects them.

"Good son, if one knows that the self is empty and there is no one who destroys the self, yet there is still talk of 'self' because the self has not been severed, then the same applies to sentient beings and their life-span.
Good son, those sentient beings in the final age who speak of illness as the Dharma are therefore called pitiable ones;
though they exert themselves with diligence, they only increase their various ailments, and for this reason they cannot enter the pure [state]."
Pure awakening does not merely fail to produce the fruit of sainthood; moreover, it is difficult to cure the condition of mistaking illness for the Dharma.
Thus we know that if the mark of self is empty, one will be unmoved by praise or blame. One does not perceive anyone who slanders the Dharma of oneself; yet now, hearing oneself being slandered—
If one feels anger toward the Dharma and joy when praising my Dharma, this indicates that what they have taught is a doctrine of self (ātman) and not a doctrine of non-self (anātman).
This is because their mark of self (ātmagrāha) has not yet been severed.
If even the coarse mark of self cannot yet be severed, how much less so the subtle mark of sentient beings and the extremely subtle mark of a life-span? Thus, it is said:

Knowing that while there is one self, the four marks all persist—and since these four marks are the root of the sicknesses of sentient beings—it would indeed be pitiable to take this very sickness as the Dharma.
Therefore, if the four marks are not eliminated, even the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) becomes a poisonous drug;
even if one exerts oneself with diligent effort, it will do nothing but aggravate all illnesses. This is...
Therefore, they are unable to enter pure awakening; it is not that awakening rejects them.

Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks. Taking the understanding and the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata as their own cultivation, they ultimately fail to achieve success.
Or there may be sentient beings who have not attained yet claim to have attained, and have not realized yet claim to have realized. Seeing...
Those who seek superior progress give rise to jealousy in their hearts. Because those sentient beings have not yet severed self-love, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
Furthermore, it is not merely that they take illness as the Dharma; moreover, relying on illusion to speak of awakening, they treat what belongs to others as their own.
Because they do not understand these four characteristics, they take what the Tathāgata has understood to be their own understanding, and what the Tathāgata has practiced to be their own practice.
As it is said: "To rely on the sūtras to explain the meaning is an enemy to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like a person counting another's treasures; he himself does not possess even half a coin. Likewise, if one does not practice the Dharma, much learning is also [of no avail]."
It is so. How could one know that those who enter through the gate are not the family treasures and will ultimately achieve nothing?
There may be sentient beings who, having not yet attained Bodhi, claim they have already attained it; who, having not realized Nirvana, say they have already realized it;
and who, upon seeing those who excel and progress, instead give rise to envy. Are these truly those who have realized or attained the truth? These are all... [not so].
By severing self-love, one naturally gives rise to obstacles; for this reason, one cannot enter pure awakening. It is not that awakening rejects them.
Good son, when sentient beings in the final age hope to achieve the Way, do not let them seek enlightenment, lest it only increase their learning and [their attachments].

Do not increase your views; rather, you should diligently subdue the afflictions. Arouse great courage and vigor so that what has not been attained may be attained, and what has not been severed may be severed.
Do not give rise to greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, or jealousy toward objects. Let all attachment to self and others be completely extinguished.
The Buddha says that such a person will gradually achieve accomplishment, seek out virtuous friends, and not fall into false views. If...
If one gives rise to hatred and attachment toward that which is sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
This demonstrates the method for entering awakening. Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age desire to become Buddhas or patriarchs, yet they do not allow their sincere hearts to seek enlightenment;
instead, they merely memorize words and phrases to serve as topics for conversation, thereby increasing their self-view (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
This is like the saying: "One does not satisfy oneself merely by talking about food.
After hearing the Dharma, one should apply effort and practice with a mind of diligence to subdue the afflictions.

Arousing great valor, one should enter directly with a single blade, resolutely attaining fruits not yet attained and resolutely severing delusions not yet severed. Greed, anger, craving, and pride are the root afflictions.

The three types of *daurmanasya* (distress), along with *śāṭhya* (deceit) and *īrṣyā* (envy)—these two being among the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—do not arise toward their objects if these roots of secondary affliction do not manifest.
Then this root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) naturally subsides in all respects.
Such a person gradually attains the fruit of an Arya; what delusion or confusion could prevent them from entering [the path]? Nevertheless, even though it is thus...
Having diligently practiced and cultivated, one possesses the internal primary cause; yet, one must necessarily rely upon the power of external conditions.
Only when held together by both the internal and external can realization be achieved.

Therefore, one must draw near to a wise and enlightened teacher to cleanse one's realizations and eliminate clinging attachments, ensuring that no chaff, dust, or impurities remain within the breast. When one becomes vast, empty, and transparently void, then...
One does not fall into side paths or minor tracks, but enters directly into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s perfect and universal knowledge.
If, regarding the spiritual friend one seeks, one is unable to serve them with a wholehearted devotion, but instead gives rise to love and hatred, or discriminates between their faults and failings—
As long as my faculties remain impure, I am likewise unable to enter pure awakening. Therefore, one who wishes to enter pure awakening must necessarily eliminate the four marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Pure karma, you should know: all..."
All sentient beings, due to grasping at a self and craving, undergo beginningless and deluded transmigration. Without eliminating the four kinds of marks, one cannot achieve bodhi.
Love and hatred arise in the mind; flattery and crookedness persist in all thoughts. For this reason, there is much confusion and distress, and one cannot enter the city of awakening.
If one can return to the land of enlightenment, first eliminate greed, anger, and ignorance. Let no attachment to dharmas remain in the mind, and proceed gradually.
It can be accomplished. My own body was originally non-existent; from what cause could hatred or love arise? This person seeks a virtuous friend and will never fall into wrong views.
Yet the separate mind they seek for their goal ultimately cannot be accomplished.

The cities of awakening and the lands of enlightenment are all metaphors for the Dharma-nature realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*). As for "attachment to dharmas" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), it is spoken of in contrast to "attachment to self" (*ātmatṛṣṇā*).

Attachment to self is an afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) severed by those of the Two Vehicles; attachment to dharmas is an obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) severed by Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*).
Those who sever attachment to self achieve the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; those who sever attachment to dharmas achieve Bodhi. Furthermore, regarding this attachment...
The mind arises from the self. If one knows that the self does not exist, how can hatred and love arise?
If a practitioner does not harbor attachment to dharmas, they possess the correct cause;

by further seeking virtuous friends as external conditions, they will be guided toward the right path and shall never fall into wrong views. Regarding the virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) whom one seeks:
If one gives rise to hatred and attachment toward extremes, one will likewise be unable to enter pure awakening;
this is because inferior persons lack sincerity and thus fail to attain its essence.
*The Near Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhi Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*, Part Five.
In the sixth fascicle of the *Exegesis on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Dafangguang Yuanjue Xingduo Luo Liaoyi Jing Jineshi),
composed by the Venerable Tongrun of Er Leng-an: At that time,
the Bodhisattva Pujue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
He circumambulated the Buddha three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you have eloquently expounded upon the maladies of dhyāna, causing this great assembly to attain what they have never experienced before. Our minds are now cleared and we have attained great peace and stability.

World-Honored One, as sentient beings in the final age gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, the worthy and holy ones remain hidden while false teachings flourish. What kind of person should these sentient beings seek?"
"By relying on what Dharma? By practicing what conduct? By removing what illness? How should one resolve the mind?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.

Although the four characteristics have already been clarified and the roots of illness fully revealed, if one does not recognize a person of right knowledge and vision, then one will not encounter the True Dharma, will not know the correct practice, will not eliminate the true illness, and will not give rise to the correct mind;

furthermore, one will not attain ultimate accomplishment, for the awakened mind has not yet become universal. It is for this reason that Pujue (Universal Awakening) seizes the opportunity to pose his question. "Speak quickly of Chan!"
"Regarding 'the sick': this refers to the statement that attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is an extremely profound illness. Meditation itself is fundamentally without illness;

it is because practitioners of meditation take illness as their method and fail to find its gateway that they cannot enter it, and thus it is described as an illness. Now, having heard this once, the root of the illness has been eliminated;
therefore, the mind is vast and open, entirely free from doubt or obstruction, and one attains great peace and stability."
Thus it is. The World-Honored One now formally requests: A teacher is that which people take as a mold; from them arises the source of both the heterodox and the orthodox.
Therefore, one must inquire and seek what kind of spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) so that one does not fall into false views.

This is truly because the teacher acts as a guide and the teaching serves as a carpenter’s line. Thus, even after attaining realization, the ancients insisted that one must necessarily encounter a true spiritual friend.
Consciousness—only by piercing deeply and applying painful prodding to that which one values most can one enter the True Dharma; otherwise, one falls into a conceptual trap. Thus, Yaoshan said:
"As soon as there is something valued, it becomes a conceptual trap. Therefore, he asked, "Upon what dharma do you rely?

Furthermore, since practice is undertaken to cultivate virtue, one must not fail to select its essentials; thus he asked, "What kind of practice do you perform? This refers to that upon which one relies.
If one clings to these dharmas and does not let go, then the medicine becomes a disease and the illness is mistaken for the Dharma;
this is not only useless but actually harmful. Therefore, he asks: "How is illness to be removed? To resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is the beginning of entering the Path.
Whether it is heterodox or orthodox, Great or Small, everything depends entirely on this first step. Therefore, he asks: "How does one resolve the mind? If one understands these five...
Once one's own eyes have become clear, one can also universally awaken all who are blind and lead them onto the right path.
If one's own eyes are not clear, this is like leading the blind with the blind; there are none among them who do not fall into pits and ditches.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

That you are able to question the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation is capable of bestowing upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way, enabling those beings to attain the holy path.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Then Universal Enlightenment...
The Bodhisattva received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.

One who possesses the fearless eye of the Way is said to be endowed with five kinds of natures; such a person can distinguish between dragons and snakes, and between the heterodox and the orthodox, and is decisively able to advance straight ahead without giving rise to cowardice.

"Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve upon the Great Mind and seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in order to practice, they should seek those who possess right knowledge and vision.
Their minds do not dwell on appearances; they do not cling to the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Although they manifest within the afflictions of the world, their minds are ever pure. They appear to have various faults while praising the holy life (brahmacarya), so as not to cause sentient beings to enter [into such faults]."
Regarding those who lack discipline: if one seeks such a person, they shall immediately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Sentient beings of the final age who see such a person should make offerings to them, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
Within the four modes of deportment, that spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) constantly manifests purity; even when manifesting various faults or afflictions, their mind remains free from pride.

How much more so regarding the accumulation of wealth, wives, children, and kinsmen! If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward such a virtuous friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment;
the flower of his mind will burst forth in brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.

First, I shall answer the first question: "What kind of person should one seek? This refers to sentient beings of the final age who, about to resolve upon the Great Mind, desire to seek a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) as a teacher upon whom to rely for cultivation.
They must first select a person of correct knowledge and vision to serve as their teacher.

Because the teacher is like a skilled physician who well understands medicinal taboos, and the teacher is like a guide who well understands what is passable and what is obstructed, one must first choose [a teacher].
What is called "right knowledge and vision" means that the mind does not dwell on the signs of form, thereby departing from the realm of ordinary beings;
nor does the mind dwell on the sign of emptiness, thereby departing from the realm of the two vehicles. Since it dwells neither in form nor in emptiness, this is precisely Bodhi.
He possesses the capacity of a bodhisattva; therefore, although he manifests the afflictions (*kleśa*), he is not defiled by them. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Though having a wife and children, he constantly cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); though appearing to have a retinue, he always delights in seclusion.
To manifest various faults while praising pure conduct is as the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* says: "He enters brothels to demonstrate the nature of desire..."

This exceeds that. All of these are cases of internal secrecy with external manifestation, employing the method of "identical activity" (*samānārthatā*) to gather others, so as not to allow sentient beings to enter into non-discipline (*aśīla*).

If one seeks such a person of right knowledge and vision to serve as a teacher, then one can have their nails and wedges pulled out, their bones and marrow transformed, and achieve *bodhi*. Therefore, one should encounter such a person of right knowledge and vision.
One should offer service with all one’s heart, not sparing even body or life, as exemplified by those such as Śvetaketu who sacrificed their bodies and the deity who severed his own arm.
This spiritual friend possesses great efficacy; he is capable of both the ultimate and the provisional.

At times, he transforms people through favorable circumstances, manifesting pure appearances, and his compassion is overflowing. At other times, he receives people through adverse circumstances, manifesting...
When greed and anger manifest, the staff and the shout are deployed in rapid succession. What is called "either conforming or opposing" is all termed "superior.

This includes, for example, the abuse of Ciming, the staff of Deshan, the shout of Linji, the flesh of Fenyang, the pigeon of Master Zhi, and the wine of Yu Xian—all of which were acts of "inverse practice.
When encountering such circumstances, one must not immediately give rise to arrogance.
Because pride prevents the arising of reverence, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One should regard all teachers and elders as if they were the World-Honored One.
If they can explain profound meanings and resolve one's doubts, thereby benefiting me, then one should honor them with all one's heart and mind, without dwelling on their faults.
It is like a tattered bag containing jewels; one does not refuse to take the jewels because of the poor quality of the bag. Furthermore, it is like...
When traveling at night through a perilous path, one may encounter a person holding a torch; one should not refuse its light simply because that person is wicked.

Even if they manifest all manner of faults and afflictions, one ought not to give rise to a mind of arrogance, let alone become conceited merely because they possess wealth, a wife, children, and servants. If one serves a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra)...
When conceit arises, one immediately examines this mind to see that it remains steady and unshakable, free from love and hate, and uniform in its single characteristic.
One will certainly be able to ultimately enter pure awakening. The flower of awakening will spontaneously manifest, perfect and pure, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
"Good son, the sublime Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should be free from the four illnesses. What are the four illnesses?

First is the illness of effort (*kṛta-vyādhi*). If there is someone who says, 'I shall perform various practices upon my original mind in order to seek perfect enlightenment,' this is called an illness because the nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through effort. Second is the illness of non-action (*anābhoga-vyādhi*). If..."
Furthermore, there are those who speak as follows: "We now neither sever saṃsāra nor seek nirvāṇa;
we harbor no thoughts of arising or ceasing regarding either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra. We leave everything as it is, following the nature and desires of all phenomena while seeking perfect enlightenment.

Because that nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that can be left as it is, this is called a sickness. Third is the sickness of cessation. If, furthermore, there is someone who speaks thus:
They speak thus: "I have now permanently stilled all thoughts within my own mind and attained the tranquil equanimity of all natures.
In seeking *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment), that nature of perfect enlightenment is not something to be attained through cessation; therefore, [this practice] is called a 'disease.
Fourth is the disease of extinction (*nirodha-gada*). If there is another person who speaks thus: "I have now forever severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), and my body and mind are ultimately empty."
There is nothing at all; how much less so the false realms of sense organs and objects? All things are eternally quiescent.

If one seeks perfect enlightenment (bodhi) therein, that nature of perfect enlightenment is not a state of quiescence; therefore, such seeking is called a "sickness. One who is free from these four sicknesses knows purity.
To contemplate in this way is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called false contemplation.

This answers the second question regarding "by means of what dharmas. The sublime Dharma realized by this spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) must be free from the four illnesses to be considered the True Dharma.
These four illnesses are precisely the three contemplations previously practiced and the Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) of non-cultivation and non-realization;
because they were grasped and not transformed, they turned into illnesses. Therefore, one should not give rise to a mind of attachment.
The illness itself is the medicine; if one gives rise to a mind of attachment, the medicine becomes the illness.

This is what the ancient masters meant when they said that "the entire body is medicine and the entire body is illness. To speak of "becoming ill" refers to that which is produced by taking the medicine of samādhi.
That person thinks to themselves: "This nature of Perfect Enlightenment must be achieved through diligent effort and arduous practice, performing various deeds to deliver all sentient beings.
They do not realize that this nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally not something to be produced;
this wondrous, spiritual essence does not undergo conditioning or refinement. How could one falsely attain it by practicing various deeds? This is...
They lose their natural truth and instead engage in the boring out of apertures; therefore, this is called "acting as a sickness.

To speak of "accepting the sickness" means it is accomplished by taking the medicine of the pure, fundamental non-existence of cultivation and realization within Perfect Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*).

Their intention is to claim that birth-and-death is fundamentally empty and need not be further severed, and that nirvana is fundamentally quiescent and need not be sought. Therefore, they do not seek nirvana and do not sever [birth-and-death].
In the cycle of birth and death, they act according to their own whims and depart following conditions, conforming to the nature of all phenomena.

Encountering greed, they become greedy; meeting anger, they become angry; finding clothing, they put it on; encountering food, they eat. They have no sense of restraint and do not avoid reproach or censure.
To give rise to such a mind while seeking Perfect Enlightenment is to rely on one's innate nature and fail to practice. Constantly...

Dwelling within illusion and transformation, one cannot attain liberation; therefore, this is called the "sickness of indulgence. The Commentary states: Whereas previously one was driven about in search of the Buddha, here one lets the body and mind run wild.
Even if one does not restrict oneself to good or evil, one nonetheless falls into the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

How could the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove be the Great Way? How could the Four White-Headed Elders be sages? They were still mired in the heavens of desire; how could they have been darkly attuned to the essence of awakening?
When a practitioner reaches this point, they may drown in water or sink their vessel. One should therefore exercise self-vigilance and harbor no attachment to this affliction.
Curing this affliction is accomplished by taking the medicine of *śamatha*. In that state, one considers the mind to be eternally stilled and at peace, like wood or stone;

Good son, sentient beings in the final age who wish to seek Perfect Enlightenment should resolve their minds and speak these words:

"Bound. This is because if one belongs to the eight consciousness-kings, there is bondage; once there is bondage, there is defilement, and one cannot attain equanimity.

Progressing gradually and increasingly, one eventually comes to know even a single drop of rain from hundreds of thousands of worlds as clearly as if seeing it with one's own eyes,
