because it pierces through the nostrils of all Buddhas. Regarding "that which is protected by the Tathāgatas": among all treasures...
The Dharma Jewel is supreme, for the Tathāgata protects and cherishes it as a black dragon guards its wish-fulfilling jewel.

Those who take refuge in the Bodhisattvas rely upon this to establish their person and depend upon this to deliver sentient beings. It is the pure eye, for it is the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa and the treasury of the true Dharma-eye.
"Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) means that its essence is great and its virtues are square and perfect.

Because its application is vast, why is its virtue described as "square" (fang)? It means that within the great essence, the intrinsic virtues of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are fully present.
These are not that, nor is that these; each has its own fixed name and its own specific antidote.
*Dhāraṇī* is called "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*) because it encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings.
It is "definitive meaning" because not a single character is established and not a single meaning is omitted. It is the "secret king" because it is close at hand yet invisible when looked upon;
it is profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it. It is the "decisive realm" wherein the myriad phenomena...
Because it is sealed by a single dharma like an elephant; because the dharma-gate of self-realization cannot be altered by external things.
The four names above all manifest the meaning of the unchanging nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The name below manifests the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya*).
Regarding the differentiation of the intrinsic nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*: because the *tathāgatagarbha* does not maintain its own nature but follows conditions, it becomes the five [dharmas].
Because of the distinctions in their natures, that which reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata refers to the fact that all twelve bodhisattvas have perfected *bodhi* (enlightenment).
That only the Buddha-Tathāgata can fully proclaim it is because the ultimate true reality (*tathatā*) belongs solely to the Tathāgata, and only the Tathāgata can fully proclaim it;
for the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
"If all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely on this to practice, gradually advancing until they reach the stage of Buddhahood"—
this answers the question as to what stage is reached. That is to say, practitioners rely on these five names to resolve their minds and practice,
gradually advancing from the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages, up to the stage of Buddhahood.
This sutra also flows forth from the initial aspiration for enlightenment all the way to the stage of Buddhahood; that is to say, it is to realize the truth by relying on the names.
Good son, this sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna. Sentient beings with sudden capacities awaken through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice gradually.
It is like the great ocean, which does not reject even small streams, down to those as tiny as mosquitoes and gadflies.
"Those asuras who drink its water all obtain full satisfaction.

How should this answer be upheld? This sutra universally covers the three capacities, encompassing both the sudden and the gradual teachings, just like the great ocean which can carry both the giant Kunlun and the great Peng birds, and can also carry small fish and tiny shrimp; when rivers and streams enter it,"

It does not refuse; even when entering through ditches and channels, it meets no obstruction. Thus, from the minute mosquito and gadfly to the great asura, all obtain full satisfaction according to their capacity.
One may thus know that whether this sutra is upheld by the small or the great, its efficacy is never lost.
"Good son, suppose there were someone who filled a trichiliocosm entirely with the seven precious jewels and used them as a gift of alms;
this would not equal a person hearing the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning.

Good son, suppose there were someone who taught as many sentient beings as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers to attain the fruit of Arhatship; this would not equal a person proclaiming [this teaching]..."

This sutra analyzes half a verse. "Good son, if there is another person who hears the name of this sutra and their faith is not confused, you should know that such a person has not planted roots of merit and wisdom under only one or two Buddhas.
Rather, they have planted various roots of goodness under all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having heard the teachings of this sutra."

This answers the question regarding the cultivation of merit. Although the merit from giving away the seven treasures of a great trichiliocosm is already immeasurable, it does not equal that of hearing even a single meaning of this sutra.
This is because one is a worldly treasure and the other is a Dharma-treasure; worldly treasures are finite, while the Dharma-treasure is inexhaustible.
Worldly treasures are subject to destruction, whereas the Dharma-treasure is indestructible. Thus, [the merit of teaching] hundreds of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
The merit obtained from attaining the four fruits of the path is already inexhaustible; yet it does not equal that of a person who proclaims even half a verse of this sutra.
This is because one is a *musāragalva* gem and the other is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); and because one is a divine *kumbhīra* and the other is a divine dragon (*nāga*).
Therefore, not only those who hear this entire sutra and attain full understanding [attain the merit of] countless *saṃsāra*-sands of Buddhas.

As for those who have planted roots of goodness—those whose minds are not confused upon hearing these five names—it is only those who have come from the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who can hear this sutra inscribed upon their ears. How difficult it is to hear the Dharma!

"You, son of good family, should protect those practitioners in the final age, ensuring that evil Māras and various heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies and minds or cause them to fall into despondency and retreat."

This is the answer for those who uphold this sutra: "In the final age, if there are those who practice according to this sutra, you all should secretly provide supernatural protection and support so that demons and heretics do not disturb their minds or cause them to become discouraged.
The section on the Main Teaching is concluded.
At that time, within the assembly were eighty thousand Vajras, including Agnīśikhara-vajra, Vajra-pramardana-vajra, and Nīlambā-vajra, together with their retinues.
They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if in the future final age there are sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Great [Dharma]...”
We shall protect [you] as we would our own eyes, even unto the site of enlightenment and wherever you practice the path.
We, the Vajras, together with our retinues, will personally guard you morning and night, ensuring that you do not regress.
In your home, may all calamities and obstacles be forever absent, may pestilence be extinguished, and may wealth and treasures abound so that there is never a lack.
The following is the section on the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*). First, the dissemination is protected by the Vajragarbha deity.
"Fire-Head Vajra" refers to Ucchuṣma. Because this sutra is the essence that is non-illusory and indestructible, it is protected by the Vajragarbha deity.
"Free from calamities and obstacles" means having severed the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). "Eliminating pestilence" means being free from the four diseases.
Those who possess abundant wealth and treasures are endowed with the jewel of omniscience.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, the twenty-eight kings of the heavens, Sumeru the king of mountains, the heavenly kings who protect the nations, and others [were present].
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, constantly ensuring they remain in peace and security, so that their minds do not regress.”
This refers to the Heavenly Kings who protect and circulate [the Dharma]. "The twenty-eight heavens" generally indicates the twenty-eight heavenly kings of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
"Sumeru, King of Mountains" specifically clarifies Śakra. "Heavenly Kings who Protect the Nation" specifically clarifies the Four Great Kings.
"Whose minds do not regress" means that there are no demonic disturbances and their minds are not troubled or moved.

At that time, a powerful ghost-king named Kimpaka, together with one hundred thousand ghost-kings, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra.
Day and night I shall attend to them so that they do not fall back or become discouraged. Within a distance of one yojana of where such a person dwells, if there should be..."
If ghosts and spirits invade his realm, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.

These three ghost kings provide protection. The Kumbhāṇḍas feed on the vital essence and blood of humans; they are as swift as the wind and govern all ghosts and spirits, and are therefore called "Kings.
Thus, one should know that for those who can uphold this sutra, even the malevolent ghosts and spirits shall all become [their protectors].
If even those who protect the Dharma do so, how much more so the benevolent deities? For practitioners, one should only fear that the power of the Way is not firm;
one need not fear that ghosts and spirits will not provide protection.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the eight classes of followers, as well as the various heavens...

The King, the Brahma Kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it, and thus it was propagated among the fivefold assembly.
